title: Ukraine urges US to speed up interceptor deliveries as Russia targets power grid
excerpt: Ukraine’s foreign minister said he had urged Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday to accelerate deliveries of interceptors as Russia ramps up attacks on energy infrastructure to break Ukrainian m...
body_text:
Ukraine’s foreign minister said he had urged Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday to accelerate deliveries of interceptors as Russia ramps up attacks on energy infrastructure to break Ukrainian morale during the winter months.

Speaking after talks with Rubio on the sidelines of a G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris, Andrii Sybiha told Reuters he had pressed Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow even as diplomatic efforts to end the war took place in Abu Dhabi.

“We should work on the peace track, but in parallel we should continue to pressure Russia,” he said in an interview.

Sybiha said he had requested additional support for Ukraine’s battered energy grid and more air-defence interceptors, while confirming that U.S. intelligence sharing and military assistance through the Priority Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) program remained in place.

“I raised the issue of how we could speed up some supply, how we could find a proper way to maybe front-load something, and how we could try to find additional quantities,” he said.

His remarks come as Kyiv seeks assurances of continued Western military backing while supporting diplomatic efforts to explore limited confidence-building measures with Moscow.

Commenting on the U.S.-mediated talks now underway between Ukrainian and Russian officials in Abu Dhabi, Sybiha said: “Ukraine has serious intentions … We try to use any opportunity to speed up peace efforts and to make peace closer.”

He said Ukraine remained prepared to discuss a range of de-escalatory measures, including ceasefires covering the Black Sea and energy infrastructure.

Sybiha said proposals for a Black Sea ceasefire had been conveyed to Russia through intermediaries including Turkey, Egypt and India, but added he was “not so optimistic” about progress and was still awaiting a response from Moscow.

Sybiha reiterated Kyiv’s accusations that Russia is deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure ahead of winter.

“[Russian President Vladimir Putin] tries to break our spirit during the winter,” he said.

Russia denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war, now well into its fifth year.

Sybiha was attending a meeting in Paris of foreign ministers from the Group of Seven, which comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States, as well as the European Union.

He said the cost of the war would rise significantly in 2027 and expressed hope that Kyiv could secure longer-term financial commitments from its partners by the end of the year.

“We need macrostability,” he said. “For domestic purposes, it keeps the spirit of our people strong when they understand that at least for one to two years we have long-term commitments.”

Sybiha said his family in Kyiv — including three children — like most Ukrainians, often had only a few hours of electricity a day.

“It means no heating, no water, no sanitation, so it’s a big challenge for us,” he added.

title: Meet the Peaky Blinders, Ukraine's drone unit protecting a devastated front-line city
excerpt: The BBC's Jonathan Beale reported from inside Slovyansk, one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Done...
body_text:
The BBC's Jonathan Beale reported from inside Slovyansk, one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.

The town has become almost uninhabitable and has been under heavy bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.

Members of a Ukrainian drone unit that call themselves Peaky Blinders, named after the cult BBC TV series, have taken on the task of intercepting Russian drones.

Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.

title: Spain braces for nationwide strike as anger over housing, costs boils over
excerpt:
Spain is bracing for a nationwide general strike over soaring rents and the cost of living, as a deepening housing crisis fuels social unrest weeks before a crucial election.

The 24-hour walkout due ...
body_text:
Spain is bracing for a nationwide general strike over soaring rents and the cost of living, as a deepening housing crisis fuels social unrest weeks before a crucial election.

The 24-hour walkout due to begin at midnight on Wednesday was called by Spain’s two biggest unions – the Comisiones Obreras (CCOO) and Union General de Trabajadores (UGT) – under their slogan: wages, housing, prices. The last time the pair called a general strike was in 2012 when the country was engulfed in an austerity crisis.

The protest will disrupt transport, schools, healthcare and other public services across Spain. Flight cancellations and delays are also expected, while public transport in major cities will operate at reduced capacity.

Schools, hospitals, shops and other services could also face closures or reduced staffing, although minimum services will be maintained in essential sectors.

The action follows the September eviction of an 87-year-old, who has since passed away, from her home in Madrid, after her corporate landlord increased the rent. Images of Maricarmen Abascal being forcibly removed on a stretcher struck a nerve. The moment led to nationwide demonstrations and encampments in a wave of protests that also fuelled a political crisis, prompting the government to call the November 29 snap elections.

Wednesday’s strike could help the government bring the housing crisis back to the centre of the political debate, said Luke Stobart, a political analyst who writes about social movements and politics in Spain.

“(Socialist Prime Minister Pedro) Sanchez has been famous for taking risks in the past, and he’s often been quite successful when he’s taken them. And he knows that if you have a general strike before elections, that will force everyone to talk about housing. And that is happening – it is helping to keep housing at the centre of the debate in the run-up to the elections,” Stobart said.

The country has 750,000 fewer homes than it needs, according to the Bank of Spain, which estimates that the gap could exceed one million by 2028.

Rents have rocketed to an average of 1,176 euros ($1,318) per month, and the average salary of a young person is 1,190 euros ($1,333), according to data collated by the Spanish Youth Council.

Many struggling to make ends meet are forced to live in overcrowded shared flats or stay with their parents.

Spain is not alone, as other European nations witness weekly mass protests over costs and living conditions.

While Sanchez has not explicitly endorsed the strike, he praised collective action as the driving force behind the country’s social gains.

“Your eight-hour working day. Your pension. Your public healthcare. None of this fell from the sky. They were collective achievements. We will not let anyone take them away from us,” the prime minister said in a video message on Monday.

He believes his government has more to offer on social policies than political opponents.

But his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) has lost support in recent months over its handling of the migration crisis in Ceuta. It is also plagued by a series of corruption scandals involving Sanchez’s inner circle and family members.

Recently, a deadly train crash in early November gave the opposition, the conservative Popular Party (PP) and far-right Vox, an opportunity to shift the national debate towards transport safety and what they described as government incompetence.

The crash, which occurred on the same railway line as another deadly accident less than a year earlier, killed 69 people. Transport Minister Oscar Puente, a senior PSOE figure and close ally of Sanchez, resigned.

The PP is ahead in opinion polls and could form a government with Vox, a prospect that would bring a far-right party into Spain’s national government for the first time since the end of Francisco Franco’s 1939-1975 dictatorship.

Both opposition parties have dismissed the strike as politically motivated, accusing unions of targeting the opposition ahead of the election. They have also criticised its timing, coming a day after the state funeral for the victims of the train accident.

Stobart said the strike has multiple layers, with different left-leaning groups putting forward a different narrative.

Some are critical of the government. These include Basque unions ELA and LAB, Galicia’s CIG, and Spain’s CGT, which have accused the regional and national governments of failing to tackle housing speculation.

“It’s not clear whether the big trade union leaders and the government are going to be able to control the narrative,” Stobart said, warning that the protests could develop into a broader wave of social unrest, as seen in France and Italy, potentially backfiring on the government.

title: Iran backs nuclear treaty even as hardliners raise prospect of bomb
excerpt: Tehran, Iran – Iran says it has not suspended its commitments under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), but as mediated talks to end the war with the United States continue, ...
body_text:
Tehran, Iran – Iran says it has not suspended its commitments under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), but as mediated talks to end the war with the United States continue, broad international inspections of Iranian sites remain far off.

Following US and Israeli attacks on Iran’s main nuclear facilities in and assassinations of senior leaders, Iranian authorities have increasingly discussed the possibility of abandoning the international treaty and building a nuclear bomb.

US President Donald Trump’s threats to attack the underground Pickaxe Mountain complex near the Natanz nuclear facility and other sensitive sites have only emboldened hardliners in Tehran to demand a shift in the country’s nuclear doctrine – under assassinated Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, nuclear weapons were officially forbidden.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei emphasised to reporters during a news conference in Tehran on Monday that the Islamic Republic remains committed to the NPT, despite restricting cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the United Nations’ nuclear watchdog.

“Other parties have imposed conditions, namely the attacks by the US and Zionist regime against our nuclear facilities which have caused issues concerning implementation of safeguards commitments,” he said, in reference to Israel.

“As long as this situation continues, we cannot act like normal circumstances in our cooperation with the agency,” Baghaei said about the IAEA, while also renewing Tehran’s criticism of its director, Rafael Grossi.

But the spokesman confirmed that new IAEA inspections were conducted days earlier at the Bushehr nuclear power plant.

The electricity generation plant, built in cooperation with Russia and under development for new phases, is the only facility still accessible to the agency, as it was not directly bombed during the war. US warplanes did, however, attack the perimeter of the plant several times and caused damage, prompting partial evacuation of Russian personnel, who have yet to fully return.

IAEA chief Grossi told the UN Security Council in late October that the body was unable to verify Iran’s nuclear material because Tehran “has not provided the requested information and access”.

Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at the International Crisis Group, said Tehran is keeping one foot inside the NPT and the other near the exit.

“Allowing inspections at Bushehr is a low-cost gesture designed to keep diplomacy alive and hardliners at bay, while preserving leverage over the underground nuclear sites that matter most,” he told Al Jazeera.

Those sensitive sites include the Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan facilities, among others.

Seyed Hossein Mousavian, a visiting researcher at Princeton University and a former Iranian nuclear negotiator, said Iran’s position “reflects a distinction between honouring its NPT commitments and permitting inspections of facilities that have been bombed”.

Mousavian said the IAEA had no established inspection protocol for nuclear facilities damaged by military attacks, and pointed out that the Iranians fear that IAEA access to sensitive sites would lead to information being shared with the US and Israel that could then be used in future attacks.

“Tehran views restrictions on broader inspections as a security concern rather than necessarily a rejection of its NPT obligations,” he said.

Iran has had one of the most scrutinised nuclear programmes in history, and its international obligations are governed by several treaties and UN resolutions.

The NPT establishes the fundamental rules against nuclear proliferation, while recognising the right to peaceful nuclear energy. A separate safeguards agreement with the IAEA sets out how the agency monitors Iran’s nuclear activities to make sure it isn’t moving towards weapons development. Subsidiary arrangements, UN Security Council resolutions and nuclear agreements have fulfilled additional requirements.

As a party to the NPT, Iran’s peaceful nuclear-use rights are recognised, and it is allowed to undertake peaceful exchanges and receive assistance with nuclear development.

In exchange, the country commits not to receive, manufacture or otherwise acquire nuclear weapons, and to accept safeguards and information sharing in its territory.

Withdrawal requires a notice after a decision has been made that “extraordinary events” have “jeopardised the supreme interests” of the country.

However, the treaty does not protect from conventional military attack, and this gap between promised peaceful-use benefits and actual vulnerability has been at the centre of the appeal by domestic hardliners to leave the NPT.

But such considerations have not been limited to a handful of hawkish figures.

Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei has publicly deliberated the possibility of abandoning the treaty on multiple occasions. Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said earlier this week that the organisation “will create the necessary preparations” if the Islamic Republic goes through with the decision to change its nuclear doctrine.

Regional mediators like Qatar and Pakistan continue to relay messages between Iran and the US to prevent another all-out war, although analysts have warned that escalation is likely over the coming months.

Tehran has maintained that it will not allow its highly enriched uranium to be taken out of the country, but remains open to downblending it under international supervision inside Iran. It has also said it will not abandon enrichment altogether, but can accept a limit on enrichment as it did with the 2015 nuclear deal that US President Donald Trump unilaterally abandoned in 2018, during his first term in office.

Arriving at a deal that thoroughly addresses Iran’s nuclear programme would also require a resolution to hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz and beyond, something that is unlikely to materialise in the foreseeable future.

“Tehran might be willing to open the door a crack in exchange for tangible American concessions, but it is unlikely to surrender its most valuable nuclear bargaining chips upfront,” the Crisis Group’s Vaez said.

The expert added that a preliminary deal could potentially unlock limited, phased inspections based on the 2025 Cairo agreement between Iran and the IAEA.

The agreement came several months after the US and Israel bombed Iran’s nuclear facilities during the 12-day war of June 2025. It envisaged restored access for agency inspectors to all Iranian facilities, if case-by-case permission is granted by the country’s Supreme National Security Council.

But it was never enforced, and was followed by tensions that led to the US and Israel attacking Iran again on February 28.

“Restoring meaningful transparency over Iran’s nuclear programme will require a larger bargain on enrichment, stockpiles and sanctions relief,” Vaez said.

But Mousavian said Tehran would want more than just a preliminary agreement like the Cairo deal.

“Such cooperation would require a comprehensive agreement that addresses the overall security and nuclear issues; without it, inspections of the bombed sites are unlikely,” he said.

title: Pentagon can’t track millions of F-35 spare parts, watchdog finds
excerpt:
The Pentagon is still struggling to track millions of F-35 spare parts worth billions of dollars years after government watchdogs first exposed problems with its tracking system, a new report states.
...
body_text:
The Pentagon is still struggling to track millions of F-35 spare parts worth billions of dollars years after government watchdogs first exposed problems with its tracking system, a new report states.

The Government Accountability Office said Monday that while the DoD’s F-35 program “is the costliest in its history,” the department “struggles to account” for its parts.

The government watchdog described the DoD’s records for F-35 parts as “outdated, inaccurate, and incomplete” and said “DoD has made minimal progress in attaining and maintaining accountability for F-35 parts” since issues were first brought to light seven years ago.

The report follows several audits since 2019 by the GAO and the Department of Defense Inspector General, which revealed numerous problems.

Unlike most aircraft, the F-35 program largely relies on a joint pool of spares – such as engines and tires – for the U.S. Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps, as well as international customers.

As of March 2026, this pool comprised approximately 26 million spare parts valued at around $31 billion, the GAO reported. About 17,000 parts – worth up to $2.5 billion – were not recorded in the Pentagon’s property and logistics management platform, the Enterprise Logistics Management System.

In 2023, the GAO reported that one prime contractor lost more than 1 million F-35 spare parts worth more than $85 million from 2018 to 2022. As of March 2026, the F-35 Joint Program Office still did not know the status of the items.

The F-35 has two prime contractors: Lockheed Martin for the airframe, and Pratt & Whitney for the engines. The U.S. Air Force awarded Lockheed Martin a $1.6 billion contract for more spare parts in July.

Issues still plague inventory tracking systems used by the F-35 Joint Program Office.

“For instance, records of F-35 parts in the F-35 program’s accountable property system of record remain unreliable, since they do not reflect real-time changes and are inaccurate and incomplete,” the GAO report states.

Nor can the Enterprise Logistics Management System track joint spare parts in real-time “because ELMS does not currently interface with the two prime contractors’ property management systems.”

“DoD does not have its own complete records of F-35 parts, and, as a result, does not know when a part is lost unless staff at the contractor-managed or government-managed facility identifies and reports the loss,” Asif Khan, director of GAO’s financial management and assurance team, told Defense News.

For joint spares, the F-35 Joint Program Office relies on data supplied quarterly by the prime contractors, which means that “joint spares pool data in ELMS may be more than 3 months old.” Whether some F-35 spares are actually located where they should be isn’t always clear, in part because the prime contractors aren’t always aware of inventories held by their subcontractors.

Some parts were also valued quite cheaply in the contract data requirements lists, which are submitted by the prime contractors quarterly.

“Almost 6 percent of records of F-35 parts, also from the December 2025 CDRL, showed an acquisition cost of $0.01 or less, also indicating a possible data quality error,” the GAO noted.

“Neither records of F-35 parts in ELMS nor F-35 JPO’s inventory results are reliable for the purpose of asset accountability or financial reporting,” the report states.

Even estimating how many of the 26 million F-35 parts are missing is difficult.

“Because the F-35 JPO has not established and implemented effective procedures for monitoring losses, we are unable to provide an aggregate estimate of how many of the 26 million parts are lost,” Khan said.

The F-35 Joint Program Office should improve its procedures for recording lost parts, “including procedures for performing trend analyses that would enable mitigation of future losses,” the GAO recommended. The office should also make more use of accountable property officers who maintain records of parts, including specific training focused on the F-35 program.

Questions remain about whether an inability to track spare parts is hampering F-35 operations.

The GAO warned earlier this year that poor parts accountability is complicating efforts to improve the F-35 program. Customers have also been asking for greater transparency into the supply chain so they can properly allocate resources, Khan noted.

“For several years, we’ve been reporting that DoD cannot ensure that the prime contractor is providing sufficient readiness at a reasonable cost without an understanding of the parts it owns and how the prime contractor manages those parts,” Khan said.

Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.

title: JACKSON THOMPSON: Seattle school board authorizes legal challenge to ballot measure protecting girls' sports
excerpt:
Seattle’s school board unanimously authorized potential legal action Monday against a voter-approved measure barring biological males from girls’ school sports. (Credit: Seattle Public Schools)

Seatt...
body_text:
Seattle’s school board unanimously authorized potential legal action Monday against a voter-approved measure barring biological males from girls’ school sports. (Credit: Seattle Public Schools)

Seattle’s school board unanimously authorized potential legal action Monday against a voter-approved measure barring biological males from girls' school sports, opening another front in Washington’s fight over transgender athlete eligibility.

The 7-0 vote authorized Superintendent Ben Shuldiner to take legal action regarding Initiative 638, which bars biological males from competing in designated girls’ school sports. Two student representatives also recommended approval in separate advisory votes, according to the meeting transcript.

Board member Joe Mizrahi acknowledged his opposition to the measure before arguing that the decision before the board concerned its legal responsibilities, rather than members' personal votes.

"As a father of three daughters who play sports, I was opposed to 638," Mizrahi said.

He said the district had received messages from people urging it to protect students and others asking it to support the initiative and respect the election result.

JACKSON THOMPSON: DEMOCRAT-APPOINTED JUDGES HAND LETITIA JAMES WIN OVER COUNTY TRYING TO PROTECT GIRLS SPORTS

"I believe that what we’re doing tonight is actually both protecting students and respecting the will of voters because yes, voters supported the initiative 638 and we do take that seriously," Mizrahi said. "But our democracy also produced all those other laws."

"We can’t say we’re respecting democracy if we treat the most recent vote as a reason to ignore all the other laws that are on the books."

Initiative 638 passed in last week's election with more than 55% support, according to local reporting. It is scheduled to take effect Dec. 3. Monday’s authorization did not itself suspend the measure, and district leaders had not announced a specific legal filing or timetable following the meeting, KUOW reported.

Mizrahi argued that existing protections involving privacy, equal access and discrimination remained in place despite the initiative's passage. His remarks presented the board's rationale for seeking judicial review; they did not establish that a court had found the measure unlawful.

"It raises serious questions about equal protection, student privacy, and whether we’re creating additional barriers for female student athletes to participate in school athletics," he said. "We can’t pick one new law to follow and disregard other laws. That’s not what our oath tells us to do."

Mizrahi said the resolution would authorize the superintendent and legal counsel to ask courts to resolve those questions.

Board member Liza Rankin focused on the implementation deadline, saying school districts typically receive legal review, rulemaking and model policies before adopting their own requirements to carry out state law.

WASHINGTON STATE'S HIGH SCHOOL SPORTS LEAGUE PUTS ONUS FOR TRANS ATHLETE CONTROVERSY ON STATE LAWS

"In this case, this initiative is asking 295 districts to do that all individually to figure out how to comply with something that is legally very complicated and does conflict," Rankin said.

She said the normal process takes months and described receiving calls and messages from other school board directors asking how to implement the measure.

Rankin maintained that the board's direction was not to overturn the voters’ decision, but to obtain legal guidance on the district’s obligations.

The board had already unanimously opposed the initiative in September, citing concerns about students' dignity, privacy, safety and emotional well-being, according to the district’s website.

Supporters of the measure challenged the board’s approach Monday.

"Why are they not willing to support the will of the voters now?" supporter Dawn Land asked, FOX 13 Seattle reported.

Amy Sousa, another supporter at the meeting, argued the initiative was about fairness for girls and preserving Title IX’s promise, according to the station.

Let's Go Washington, the political committee behind the measure, told KUOW it expected state education and athletic officials to implement the requirements and protect girls’ athletic opportunities.

The initiative requires school districts and covered athletic associations to prohibit biological males from competing with or against female students in individual or team competitions designated for girls.

Students seeking to participate must provide a form or statement signed by their personal healthcare provider verifying biological sex as part of the required sports physical. Verification must rely on reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup or naturally produced testosterone levels.

The text does not require every athlete to undergo a genital examination. Opponents argue its requirements could lead to invasive examinations or additional testing, while supporters contend verification can be handled through the existing physical examination process.

The dispute follows protests over transgender participation in Washington school sports.

About a dozen Camas girls walked out of an October cross-country race involving a male competitor.

Washington Democrats said they supports outside legal challenges but will not sue themselves.

After all seven directors voted yes Monday, board President Gina Topp said the action would help the district navigate the uncertainty.

"I think getting some clarity when there is some confusion will be helpful as we move forward," Topp said.

Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

title: Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker's Upright PAC seems abandoned, website redirects to Thai gambling site
excerpt:
NFL Referees did the unthinkable last night, they called a game-changing penalty on the Kansas City Chiefs, and Craig Carton is loving every second of it.

Harrison Butker’s 2026 NFL season hasn’t bee...
body_text:
NFL Referees did the unthinkable last night, they called a game-changing penalty on the Kansas City Chiefs, and Craig Carton is loving every second of it.

Harrison Butker’s 2026 NFL season hasn’t been going to plan, and it appears his political action committee isn’t off the field.

Upright PAC, a conservative political action committee founded in September 2024 by the Kansas City Chiefs kicker, has not donated to political campaigns since its formation, while raising small sums leading up to the 2026 midterm election.

The Federal Elections Commission sees Upright PAC as still active, but Open Secrets, a nonprofit which tracks campaign finance data, noted it was not supporting any political campaigns in August 2025.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Kansas City Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker reacts after missing a field goal attempt during the first half of an NFL game against the Seattle Seahawks in Seattle on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson)

"The few thousand dollars it has raised are not enough to support candidates," David Meyers, a spokesman for Open Secrets, told The Kansas City Star.

Even more interesting: UprightPac.org now redirects to a Thai gambling website, which can be seen in an X post that’s on Butker’s account.

It’s unclear if you could still donate to Upright PAC.

The PAC was founded on Butker’s Christian values, which the website said were "under attack every day."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"In our schools, in the media, and even from our own government. But we have a chance to fight back and reclaim the traditional values that have made this country great," the website read. "We are working to mobilize Christians across this country to make sure we protect these values at the ballot box."

The launch coincided with Butker’s campaigning for U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley, the Missouri Republican senator, who was re-elected to a second term in November 2024. Money came in quickly when Butker began the PAC, raising $37,921 and spending $32,735 of it from October 2024 to the end of the year.

However, The Kansas City Star reported that Butker’s PAC didn’t spend any money on candidates in the 2024 election cycle, while 91% of the money was spent on fundraising fees for Frontline Strategies, a Republican political consulting firm based out of Pennsylvania.

Kansas City Chiefs place kicker Harrison Butker celebrates after scoring against the Los Angeles Rams during the first half of an NFL preseason football game, Saturday, Aug. 15, 2026, in Kansas City, Mo. (AP)

Since January 2025, money was also spent on the Republican fundraising platform WinRed, credit card debt, travel and an individual employed at a business co-owned by Butker for political consulting. The PAC also raised just $6,777.25 between Jan. 1, 2025, and Sept. 30, 2026, while spending $11,220.85.

The PAC had reported $741.47 cash on hand on Sept. 30.

OutKick reached out to Butker for a comment.

Meanwhile, Butker has been an issue for the Chiefs in the kicking game this season, missing seven field goals after Sunday’s 35-12 win over the New York Jets. Head coach Andy Reid said he will "address" Butker’s future with the team, adding "I’ll look at everything" to see if he will remain moving forward.

The Chiefs signed Justin Tucker to their practice squad, a controversial move given his 1-game suspension over sexual misconduct allegations by numerous massage therapists during his time with the Baltimore Ravens.

Butker dealt with controversy himself just around the time he launched the PAC, when he made a highly debated commencement speech at Benedictine College. He implied that women who graduated from college should be more excited to start a family than dive into their individual passions and careers. He also criticized Pride Month as a "deadly sin," while also attacking former President Joe Biden’s Catholic faith.

Kansas City Chiefs place kicker Harrison Butker (7) during Super Bowl LIX Opening Night at Caesars Superdome. (Kirby Lee/Imagn Images)

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Abortion was another topic he shared his views on, and the Missouri Abortion Fund has come up recently this season as they take a jab at Butker. They’re asking supporters for a $7 donation for every missed field goal – No. 7 is what Butker wears for the Chiefs.

There is a chance Butker won’t be wearing that jersey any longer in Kansas City, but his PAC might already be out the door.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

title: House Republicans urge DoJ to further investigate ‘key witnesses’ in Epstein case
excerpt:
Republicans on House panel criticize US government’s investigation into Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell

Republicans on the House oversight committee released a report on Tuesday criticizing the...
body_text:
Republicans on House panel criticize US government’s investigation into Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell

Republicans on the House oversight committee released a report on Tuesday criticizing the federal government’s handling of the investigations into Jeffrey Epstein and his associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, and called on the Department of Justice to interview “key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records”.

“The federal government has failed the survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s horrific crimes for decades,” James Comer, the Republican congressman who chairs the committee, said in a statement.

Comer also urged Congress to pass legislation he introduced that he said would “ensure witnesses and survivors and sexual crimes are not deterred from speaking freely by nondisclosure agreements”.

“We cannot undo the horrific harm inflicted on these women” he said. “But we must ensure that allegations of criminal activity are thoroughly investigated, survivors are protected, and those responsible are held accountable. The failures of the past must not be repeated.”

In a statement, a justice department spokesperson said: “the Chairman’s recommendations have already been addressed.

“The Attorney General has repeatedly said that the Epstein case is not closed and there is no statute of limitations on human trafficking” the spokesperson said.

Shortly after Comer released the report, Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the committee, called the report “misleading” and “partisan”.

“Oversight Republicans have released a report based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein” Garcia said. In his statement, he accused the justice department of continuing to “illegally withhold over 2.5m pages of documents” and said that there has been “no investigation of Ghislaine Maxwell’s transfer, and Attorney General Todd Blanche has yet to testify”.

The majority’s report outlines some of the findings that the oversight committee has come to during their 15-month long investigation into Epstein, including how Epstein cultivated and leveraged relationships with powerful people, and the failures of federal investigators and prosecutors, perhaps most notably the brokering of the controversial non-prosecution agreement and plea deal for Epstein in 2008, which led to his federal case at the time being shelved.

The panel’s investigation has included 19 transcribed interviews and seven depositions.

The report also claims that after the enactment of the Epstein Files Transparency Act last year, the justice department “failed to adequately communicate about document releases and failed to sufficiently protect survivors”.

It adds that “questions remain as to whether the DOJ has released all relevant documents”. Moreover, it states “given the speed with which EFTA records were released, several instances of deficient redaction exposed sensitive information of survivors.”

Among the recommendations, Comer is urging the justice department to further question and investigate Epstein’s longtime assistant, Lesley Groff, who testified before the panel earlier this year. Groff told lawmakers that she had no knowledge of Epstein’s crimes while working for him.

Comer also urged the justice department to investigate sexual assault allegations involving two men made by another one of Epstein’s former assistants, Sarah Kellen. Both men have denied any wrongdoing.

The Republican congressman also said the justice department should establish an “appropriate process for Epstein survivors and their representatives to access their personal files and records in unredacted form”, and more.

In a matter of weeks, Democrats will take over the committee in the 120th Congress. Garcia said: “We intend to hold real public hearings uplifting survivors and asking tough questions of the powerful men who associated with Epstein, including Donald Trump. Our work is just getting started”.

title: Trump's first Iran war escalation post-midterm losses seeks to choke off Tehran’s trade
excerpt:
Farzin Nadimi explains how the U.S. could target Iran’s remaining land routes — and why sealing them off will be a "mid- to long-term project."

President Donald Trump isn't backing off his pressure c...
body_text:
Farzin Nadimi explains how the U.S. could target Iran’s remaining land routes — and why sealing them off will be a "mid- to long-term project."

President Donald Trump isn't backing off his pressure campaign against Iran despite claims the conflict contributed to sweeping Republican losses in last week's midterm elections.

In fact, Trump is doubling down by expanding U.S. efforts to choke off the trade routes Tehran increasingly relies on as it tries to rebuild its military in the midst of war.

The new effort, dubbed Task Force Iron Gate, takes aim at a vulnerability that has persisted despite the U.S. naval blockade: the land and Caspian Sea routes Iran can use to bring in goods, dual-use technology and military supplies beyond the reach of American warships.

That approach, one expert claims, fits into a broader administration strategy of tightening the squeeze on Tehran while stopping short of restarting full-scale military operations. Meanwhile, others caution that it could produce escalation rather than an immediate diplomatic breakthrough.

IRAN VOWS ‘ASTONISHING’ STRIKES AND LIFTS MISSILE-RANGE LIMIT AS US TARGETS LAND ROUTES

An Iranian cargo truck crosses into the Pakistan-Iran border as an Iranian national flag (L) flies at half-mast at Taftan, Balochistan province on March 1, 2026 after the death of Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei amid US-Israel strikes. (Banaras KHAN / AFP via Getty Images)

"We have Operation Iron Gate that just went into effect. That means nothing comes in by land," Trump said Sunday.

But the roughly 20-person task force established at U.S. Central Command headquarters in Tampa is taking a quieter approach than Trump’s sweeping description might suggest.

"This is not a deployable special operation task force," Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told Fox News Digital, describing Iron Gate instead as a "fusion cell" coordinating military, civilian and intelligence efforts.

US ECONOMIC CHOKEHOLD ON IRAN REACHES PEAK LEVERAGE AS COLLAPSE RISKS EMERGE

Nadimi said its immediate role is likely to center on gathering intelligence about activity along Iran’s borders and building cooperation in the region that could support sanctions and other efforts to disrupt the flow of goods.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who heads the department responsible for spearheading the administration's diplomatic foreign agenda, supports taking action that could decrease military escalation.

"We don't need to conduct military strikes if we're achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure," Rubio told reporters on Tuesday.

He rejected the suggestion that the U.S. and Iran were at a stalemate, arguing that sanctions, the naval blockade and other measures were steadily weakening Tehran.

"They’re bleeding. They’re bleeding economically," Rubio said. "It is an increased pressure on Iran that continues to grow every day."

The push comes a week after an election in which the war proved a political liability for Republicans.

The Iran war was a crucial factor in the House vote for 34% of voters, according to the Fox News Voter Poll, while about six in 10 said the U.S. had made the wrong decision to take military action against Iran.

An Iranian oil tanker is seen floating on the Caspian Sea, as Iranian President Mohammad Khatami attends the opening ceremony of the Neka oil terminal on the Caspian Sea, 340 kms northwest of Tehran in Mazandaran province. (HENGHAMEH FAHIMI/AFP via Getty Images)

A separate Fox News/NORC survey conducted around Election Day found 68% said avoiding a prolonged military conflict in Iran was very important. When forced to choose, 61% said ending U.S. military involvement to lower gas prices was more important than restarting military action to stop Iran from developing nuclear weapons, while 35% chose restarting military action.

Yet four days after the election, CENTCOM announced Iron Gate, extending the administration’s pressure campaign to the land routes Tehran could use to blunt the effects of the naval blockade.

CENTCOM said the task force would coordinate efforts to disrupt advanced weapons, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illicit revenue moving across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.

"We will not allow the Iranian regime to rebuild its weapons factories or replenish its arsenal with materials smuggled across its borders," CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said in announcing the task force.

CENTCOM declined to provide additional details about how Iron Gate would operate beyond its announcement.

The challenge is the sheer scale of the territory involved.

Iran shares land borders with Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkey and Turkmenistan, spanning roughly 6,000 kilometers, according to Nadimi. While it has dozens of official border crossings, goods can also be smuggled through mountainous and desert terrain.

"It will be extremely difficult to know where and how things get in or out of Iran," Nadimi said.

Much of Iron Gate’s effectiveness will also depend on governments outside Iran.

Nadimi said the task force could build relationships with military and intelligence services in neighboring countries to identify and disrupt suspicious shipments. Turkey and Pakistan have already placed some limits on goods moving across their borders with Iran, he said, contributing to long truck lines and higher shipping costs.

But even if neighboring governments cooperate, Iran and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps are likely to look for ways around the restrictions.

Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the effort should not be judged by whether Washington can completely eliminate Iran’s overland trade.

"That is not going to mean zeroing out this trade overnight," Taleblu told Fox News Digital. Instead, he said the goal is to increase the cost of moving goods, pressure the foreign companies and individuals facilitating Iranian trade and give Washington more leverage over Tehran.

"This is literally akin to boxing in the Islamic Republic," he said.

The routes have taken on added importance as Iran’s other avenues to the outside world have narrowed.

Taleblu said Iran’s missile program remains dependent on foreign inputs including fuel precursors and high-strength steel. China and Russia are important to those flows, he said, but Iraq, Turkey and Pakistan also represent important regional routes.

The U.S. military has been enforcing a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, even during the ceasefire. (U.S. Central Command)

Nadimi described effectively restricting Iran’s land trade as a "mid- to long-term project" and predicted Tehran would initially "become more aggressive" as the pressure mounts.

"It is entirely plausible that you squeeze them hard enough that they feel like the only way to throw off the strangulation is to throw a punch," he said.

That leaves the administration trying to increase its leverage over Iran without reigniting the full-scale fighting voters strongly signaled they wanted to avoid — while Trump has publicly described the objective in much starker terms.

title: UK children’s author David Walliams accused of grooming minors
excerpt:
British comedian and children’s author David Walliams, 55, has been accused of grooming teenage fans and sexually assaulting a 15-year-old girl at his house, according to British media outlets.

The G...
body_text:
British comedian and children’s author David Walliams, 55, has been accused of grooming teenage fans and sexually assaulting a 15-year-old girl at his house, according to British media outlets.

The Guardian newspaper and ITV News broadcaster published a joint investigation on Tuesday into allegations by multiple women who gave firsthand accounts of Walliams’s alleged misconduct.

Walliams denied targeting teenagers and using his fame to manipulate them to have sex, his lawyers told the media.

Walliams said he “behaved thoughtlessly” in a letter addressing journalists, which was published by The Guardian.

“I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me,” he wrote.

Walliams is best known for starring in the BBC’s popular “Little Britain” sketch show in the early 2000s.

He authored more than 40 books, including “Mr. Stink”, “Gangsta Granny” and “The Boy in the Dress”, with his work translated into more than 50 languages and reportedly selling 50 million copies.

He was also a judge on ITV’s “Britain’s Got Talent” for years but stepped down in 2022 after apologising for making “disrespectful comments” about auditioning contestants.

Following ITV News and The Guardian’s investigation, the BBC said it was removing some programmes and would conduct a review of “all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms”.

Last year, his publisher, HarperCollins, dropped him after he faced accusations of harassing young female colleagues, which he denied.

He sought a court injunction to prevent ITV News and The Guardian from identifying him in their reporting but was blocked by a UK High Court judge last week.

Walliams’s lawyer, Sara Mansoori, told the court he had made an attempt on his life when he received letters from the publications seeking his response to the allegations. She said he later made another attempt, and he was admitted to hospital for psychiatric care last month.

A summary of the court judgement stated that some of the alleged conduct could amount to criminal offences if proven.

Nearly all the women alleging sexual misconduct by Walliams were identified only by first names.

A woman named as “Jade” said Walliams, then aged 36, contacted her through a social media page showing her age as 15 and invited her to his house in 2007. She accused him of “sexual assault” and “grooming”.

Walliams’s lawyers denied sexual contact with Jade.

A woman named as “Alex” told The Guardian that he first met her when she was a 15-year-old aspiring comedy writer and he was 32. She alleged that they engaged in sexual conduct for the first time at his home when she was 17 and he was 34.

“I think I was groomed, 100 percent. We met when I was 15, and he was promising to help me,” she said.

It is illegal in the UK for someone older than 18 to intentionally communicate with a child younger than 16 for a sexual purpose. Walliams’s lawyers told The Guardian he believed Alex was 18.

title: Democrats rally behind GOP lawmaker's Hegseth impeachment push, signal more to come in January
excerpt: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth delivers a defiant defense at the Pentagon as Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., pushes to introduce articles of impeachment against him. Fox News chief national security corresp...
body_text:
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth delivers a defiant defense at the Pentagon as Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., pushes to introduce articles of impeachment against him. Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reports on Hegseth’s response and the impeachment threat on ‘The Faulkner Focus.’

Top Democrats are lining up behind Republican Rep. Thomas Massie's effort to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth, signaling that the fight could continue when Democrats take control of Congress in January.

"Hard yes on the Hegseth impeachment resolution," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said ahead of its introduction.

The Democratic reactions online telegraph an appetite to scrutinize Trump’s administration through congressional power once their majorities are formally sworn in in January, at the start of the 120th Congress.

HAKEEM JEFFRIES DECLARES BID FOR HOUSE SPEAKER AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., speaks on impeaching Secretary of War Pete Hegseth outside the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Massie himself framed the effort as likely to be repeated in the new year.

"My Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dems control Congress," Massie said.

Already, Rep. Al Green, D-Texas — who has repeatedly introduced impeachment resolutions against President Donald Trump — urged his colleagues to expand their horizons for impeachment moments after Massie introduced his resolution.

"If the Constitution is to be honored and Congress respected, a president whom many members of Congress have declared impeachable must be impeached. Failure to do so would be another step toward making the Constitution meaningless and Congress powerless," Green wrote online.

Massie is filing eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing him of violating the War Powers Resolution in Iran and Yemen, failing to prevent civilian casualties, using lethal force in an extrajudicial manner, suppressing free speech and kidnapping a sovereign foreign leader without congressional authorization with the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

Although he didn’t mention Massie by name, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed Jeffries’ enthusiasm.

"The Senate needs to put Pete Hegseth on trial so we can remove him for his catastrophic failure in Iran," Schumer said in remarks on the Senate floor.

Even beyond a review of Hegseth’s record as war secretary, some Democrats argued that removing Hegseth would help end the conflict — a war that Democrats believe has extended far beyond Trump’s power to use the military in a conflict without a declaration of war from Congress.

"Impeach Hegseth. End the war," Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., said in a post to X.

7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks at the Association of the United States Army Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 14, 2026. (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images)

Calls for Hegseth’s impeachment have circulated among Democrats for months. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has frequently called for Hegseth to step down.

"It’s way past time," Omar, who shares her home state of Minnesota with Hegseth, said in September.

"He has made a mockery of our country; it risks our national security and it’s losing us respect."

On Monday afternoon, Omar doubled down on those calls, arguing that Hegseth had operated beyond the boundaries of his office in conducting strikes on boats off the coast of Venezuela for allegedly carrying narcotics.

"Pete Hegseth has grossly abused his position as Secretary of Defense. He is waging an illegal war in Iran, conducting extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean and continues to put innocent civilians in harm’s way," Omar said.

Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, echoed Omar’s list of grievances.

"He has caused the military and the members therein to have the lowest morale we’ve seen by his actions — firing individuals just based upon just cultural issues, basically. That kind of thing is not who we want to be a representative of us in the United States defense, and I think he should resign. And if I have to vote on it, whether it’s today or tomorrow or next week, to say that he should be impeached, I will vote so," Meeks said on Tuesday.

When asked if Democrats should renew the effort in January should Massie’s resolution face defeat, Meeks hinted that he believed so.

GOP LAWMAKER SAYS MORE QUALIFIED OFFICIALS SHOULD LEAD PENTAGON, QUESTIONS HEGSETH'S 'MORAL COMPASS'

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth takes questions from reporters during a news conference at the Pentagon on Nov. 10, 2026, in Arlington, Virginia. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"I’m not going to let it go," Meeks said. "We’re going to continue to dig into him, his involvement, his advice that led us to this illegal war in the first place."

The House must approve articles of impeachment, and the Senate must vote to convict Hegseth for him to be removed from office.

The resolution can clear the House with a simple majority but requires two-thirds of senators to affirm a guilty verdict.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Malaysia's disgraced former PM leaves jail for house arrest after embezzling millions
excerpt:
Najib smiles to reporters at the Kuala Lumpur High Court after it cleared the way for him to go home

Malaysia's disgraced former Prime Minister Najib Razak has arrived home to begin serving the rest ...
body_text:
Najib smiles to reporters at the Kuala Lumpur High Court after it cleared the way for him to go home

Malaysia's disgraced former Prime Minister Najib Razak has arrived home to begin serving the rest of a jail sentence for corruption under house arrest.

There was a big media presence at his Kuala Lumpur residence to see the 73-year-old return from prison in an SUV late on Tuesday night, escorted by a heavily armed police convoy.

Najib's return ended a four-year prison stint after he was found guilty over the embezzlement of billions of dollars from the country's sovereign wealth fund.

The 1MDB scandal brought down his government and made headlines around the world when it came to light a decade ago, embroiling prominent figures from Malaysia to Goldman Sachs and Hollywood.

Investigators estimated that $4.5bn (£3.3bn) was siphoned from the state-owned wealth fund, which Najib co-founded, into private pockets, including his own. More than $1bn allegedly ended up in accounts linked to Najib, according to prosecutors.

Najib's lawyers claim he had been misled by his advisers - in particular the financier Jho Low, who has maintained his innocence and remains at large.

Journalists jostled for a glimpse of Najib as he was driven to his home, which has been declared a federal prison

Najib's mansion in one of the capital's most exclusive neighbourhoods was declared a federal prison ahead of his homecoming on Tuesday.

Critics said his release from jail undermined efforts to fight corruption and questioned its legal basis, saying Malaysian law made no provision for house arrest.

Najib, who was prime minister from 2009 to 2018, denied wrongdoing but was convicted at two separate trials.

In the first trial he was sentenced in 2020 to 12 years in prison and jailed in 2022. The term was later halved on appeal.

In September, the King of Malaysia granted him a conditional pardon to see out the remaining two years of his sentence at home.

The transfer to his mansion was to take place on Friday but put on hold after the attorney general sought clarification of the royal decree. On Tuesday the high court ruled the house arrest was effective immediately.

Najib's party paid a $12m fine as part of the terms of the royal pardon allowing him to serve the rest of his term at home.

He was sentenced after being convicted of abuse of power, money laundering and breach of trust over 42 million ringgit ($10m; £7.7m) transferred from SRC International - a former unit of 1MDB - into his private accounts.

Najib is appealing against a 15-year prison sentence, handed down at a second trial in December 2025, in a case involving much larger sums of money. In that case he was convicted of misappropriating nearly 2.3 billion Malaysian ringgit ($569m; £422m) from the nation's sovereign wealth fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).

He is due to start serving that sentence after his house arrest ends, which is expected in August 2028.

title: Trump administration again boycotts UN human rights review
excerpt: The United States ⁠⁠has again boycotted a United Nations examination of its human rights record, drawing criticism from rights groups who say violations under President Donald Trump are surging to lev...
body_text:
The United States ⁠⁠has again boycotted a United Nations examination of its human rights record, drawing criticism from rights groups who say violations under President Donald Trump are surging to levels not seen in decades.

US representatives on Tuesday failed to show up at the UN in Geneva for the review, which all 193 UN member states undergo every four to five years.

“The delegation of the United States is not present in the room,” UN Human Rights Council President Sidharto Reza Suryodipuro, of Indonesia, announced as the session was set to begin.

The US refusal to participate prompted the UN body to delay examining the US human rights record until January. This is the second year in a row that Washington has skipped its own review.

The US withdrew from the council in February 2025 shortly after Trump began his second presidential term, claiming it was biased against Israel.

The Trump administration has been a fierce critic of the UN, withdrawing Washington from key agencies, slashing its funding and bypassing the body in launching the war on Iran.

A US State Department spokesperson said participation would imply endorsement of the council’s work.

“[We] give no credibility to the agency,” the spokesperson said.

“This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own ‘values’ as it pushes anti-American rhetoric,” the official added, without responding to allegations about the US record.

The 47-member council has not directly criticised Washington’s rights record. However, experts have expressed alarm over issues such as migrant deportations, which Washington maintains are carried out in accordance with US immigration law.

UN documents show countries had planned to raise issues such as abortion access and the death penalty.

US and international non-governmental organisations also sent nearly 200 UN submissions covering ⁠⁠topics from migration to racial discrimination.

“Enough is enough,” Jamil Dakwar, of the American Civil Liberties Union, told ⁠⁠reporters in Geneva.

“We’ve seen attacks on fundamental human rights and civil liberties unprecedented in generations,” he added.

Fourteen countries are due to take part in ⁠⁠the review process in Geneva this month. During Trump’s first term in office, the US submitted its UN Universal Periodic Review (UPR) report.

Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute who was the council’s first secretary, said the US walkout could affect the credibility of the council’s review system.

“If the predominant global power, which has always claimed to adhere to the human rights norms, doesn’t show up and doesn’t even justify why, then you are in big trouble,” he said.

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Lindsay Clancy judge denies double jeopardy motion and explains jury notes after deadlock
excerpt: Attorney Randolph Rice says prosecutors can use lessons from the first trial to refine their case. He also explains why he believes Judge William Sullivan’s order rejected Clancy’s double-jeopardy arg...
body_text:
Attorney Randolph Rice says prosecutors can use lessons from the first trial to refine their case. He also explains why he believes Judge William Sullivan’s order rejected Clancy’s double-jeopardy argument.

The Massachusetts judge overseeing the murder case against Lindsay Clancy has denied her motion to dismiss the case on double jeopardy claims, clearing the way for a retrial in the strangling deaths of her three young children that some experts believe could have a better chance at a guilty verdict.

"Because the Court concludes that there was a manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury’s deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy’s right not to be placed in double jeopardy," Judge William Sullivan wrote in a 17-page order and memorandum made public Monday.

Clancy's 26-day trial ended with a deadlocked jury on Sept. 4, with jurors later saying publicly that 11 of them accepted her insanity defense and one wanted to find her guilty of first-degree murder for what the holdout called the "methodical" slayings of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months.

LINDSAY CLANCY DEFENSE FILES MOTION TO DISMISS UNDER DOUBLE JEOPARDY GROUNDS, WITH FOCUS ON HOLDOUT JUROR

Judge William Sullivan indicates he was going to declare a mistrial before changing course and giving Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney one hour to appeal, as the jury in the case has indicated that they are unable to reach a verdict on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP, Pool)

Had the motion been granted, Clancy would not face a potential second trial, said Randolph Rice, a trial attorney and former prosecutor who is not connected to the case.

Now, he says, the order gives prosecutors a chance to address what went wrong with their case in the first trial.

"I think there's real possibility that DA [Tim] Cruz says, 'We're going back to trial ... and we have learned from our mistakes,'" Rice said.

Among the lessons learned, Rice said, may be that Plymouth County prosecutors did not show jurors enough empathy when presenting their case after 11 of the 12 jurors voted against them.

What a second trial may look like remains unclear as prosecutors have so far declined to publicly commit to bringing the same or different charges.

Lindsay Clancy looks at jurors as Judge Sullivan asks them to start deliberations for a sixth day during her murder trial on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Pool Photo by Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger)

Deliberations began on Aug. 27. On Sept. 1, they sent the first of several notes explaining their deadlocked situation.

"After many hours of deliberation, we are unable to come to a unanimous verdict," that first note said, according to Sullivan, who instructed them to keep trying.

They sent a similar note on Sept. 2, and Sullivan, without objection from lawyers on either side, read them what's known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge — an instruction given to hung jurors encouraging them to reexamine their views with an open mind while reminding jurors they should not abandon honestly held beliefs to reach their verdict.

On Sept. 3, Sullivan received another note reading, "A member of the jury is unable to follow the instructions regarding reasonable doubt. How should we proceed?"

ATTORNEY FOR LONE HOLDOUT JUROR IN LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL PUSHES BACK ON CLAIMS OF REFUSING THE LAW

Michael P. Desronvil, the juror whose refusal to join the other 11 led to a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial. (Fugitive TV)

In his order, Sullivan wrote that he was skeptical of the allegation that the holdout was "genuinely" unable to follow instructions regarding reasonable doubt and decided to hold a "limited inquiry" into each juror's ability to follow the law.

Prosecutors had opposed voir dire, and the defense asked for the holdout to be replaced with an alternate. The defense then asked for the judge to ask the foreperson to expand on what she meant in her latest note, and prosecutors objected, arguing that a question like that would improperly intrude into the deliberation process. Sullivan agreed with the commonwealth and asked each juror, "Are you able to follow my instructions on the law that were given to you earlier in the trial?"

LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR WON'T HAVE TO TURN OVER PHONE OR FACE INQUIRY, JUDGE SAYS

District Attorney Timothy Cruz leaves Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., on Thursday, September, 3, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

Each juror answered "affirmatively and credibly," Sullivan wrote.

Prosecutors and the defense agreed that the court should also reinstruct the jury, as a whole, about reasonable doubt, and Sullivan did so. Afterward, however, Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, again asked for the holdout to be replaced with an alternate, and Sullivan denied his motion.

LINDSAY CLANCY'S PUSH TO PROBE HOLDOUT JUROR HITS SNAG BEFORE PIVOTAL RETRIAL HEARING

Later on Sept. 3, the foreperson sent another note, directly accusing the holdout of ignoring reasonable doubts about the case, according to Sullivan.

LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT PRAISED AS 'AMERICAN HERO' BY LAWYER WHO SAYS HE REPRESENTS HIM

Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"[Juror Doe] has made statements acknowledging doubt but refuses to apply it to the verdict as the law states," she wrote. "This is why we cannot come to a unanimous decision."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Jurors were sent home for the day. Before deliberations resumed on Sept. 4, Sullivan and counsel on both sides discussed the latest note. Sullivan gave jurors another instruction on reasonable doubt and following the law and told them that future notes should not identify anyone's vote based on their juror number. Two hours later, with no movement in the deliberation room, Sullivan said he planned to declare a mistrial, over Reddington's objection.

He granted a one-hour stay as the defense appealed to the state's Supreme Judicial Court. A single justice summarily denied the defense’s emergency request, then Sullivan declared a mistrial.

LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT

Clancy's defense later filed a motion to dismiss on double jeopardy grounds, arguing that there was no "manifest necessity" for the court to declare a mistrial and that as a result, a new trial would violate Clancy's Fifth Amendment rights.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"Clancy contends that there was no manifest necessity for a mistrial because the Court failed to consider the alternative of inquiring into the meaning of the foreperson's notes and questioning Juror Doe to determine whether there was good cause to discharge Juror Doe," Sullivan wrote.

Juror Doe is Michael Desronvil, who came forward publicly in an interview with Fox News and said that he never had doubts about his view on Clancy's guilt.

title: First-ever Collaborative Combat Aircraft fly in formation, demonstrate air combat maneuvers
excerpt:
For the first time, the U.S. Air Force’s semi-autonomous drones flew in formation and executed air combat maneuvers.

Shield’s Hivemind, the autonomy software that “runs” Collaborative Combat Aircraft...
body_text:
For the first time, the U.S. Air Force’s semi-autonomous drones flew in formation and executed air combat maneuvers.

Shield’s Hivemind, the autonomy software that “runs” Collaborative Combat Aircraft flights, helped multiple CCAs fly in a “multi-ship” formation and execute beyond-visual-range counter-air tactics, according to a recent company release.

The release did not specify how many aircraft flew in formation or which CCA participated in the Oct. 26 exercise.

“We are excited that the aircraft and mission systems are reaching a level of integration to start showing what Hivemind can really do,” Todd Wesley, vice president of Hivemind engineering at Shield, said in the announcement.

Each flight generates data that contributes to a software release, per the statement, which supports decisions on testing and fielding.

“The combined Hivemind and aircraft software release process is nearing the point where the Air Force can fly a sortie, update the software overnight and fly again the next day,” Wesley said. “I’m grateful to the Air Force operators, engineers and test teams who fly with us and help us build trust on every flight.”

The demonstration comes as the Air Force announced its intention to have 500 combat-ready, semi-autonomous systems by 2032, with an overall fleet size of 1,000. For the CCA program, the service’s fiscal 2027 budget request included $996.5 million in procurement funding, as well as $150 million in advanced procurement for the following fiscal year and $1.37 billion in continued research and development, for a total program request of $2.37 billion.

The new Shield milestone in the CCA program comes after a F-22 raptor completed airborne tactical command and in-flight control of a YFQ-44A last month, serving as a “quarterback” and giving high-level directives to the Anduril-made CCA.

Meanwhile, Shield AI announced last week its decision to acquire Echodyne in a $5.3 billion transaction to expand the contractor’s drone-warfare capabilities.

The move to absorb Echodyne — which can produce next-generation, solid-state radar systems — was said to support Shield’s expansion into different areas of unmanned systems.

Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

title: Judge who sentenced Russell Brand praised for dispelling rape myths
excerpt:
Criminal Bar Association and campaigners hail Mr Justice Bennathan for delivering remarks with ‘piercing clarity’

The judge who sentenced Russell Brand has been praised for dispelling rape myths with...
body_text:
Criminal Bar Association and campaigners hail Mr Justice Bennathan for delivering remarks with ‘piercing clarity’

The judge who sentenced Russell Brand has been praised for dispelling rape myths with “piercing clarity”.

Mr Justice Bennathan’s sentencing remarks were particularly welcomed given that rape myths had played a part in the trial. He was also lauded for calling out “enablers” who witnessed sexual assaults by the comedian.

Sentencing Brand to 10 and a half years on Monday for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others, Bennathan said: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.”

Andrew Thomas KC, the chair of the Criminal Bar Association, and Kama Melly KC, its vice-chair, said: “We welcome the piercing clarity of the judge’s statement. Myths about rape and sexual assault must play no part in our culture or in our courtrooms. Raping or sexually assaulting someone is a crime, and blame lies entirely with the perpetrator.

“Victims of sexual violence should know that when they go to the prosecution authorities, their evidence will be judged fairly and properly. As the verdicts in Russell Brand’s case show, a properly directed jury will not be put off by a defendant’s appeal to rape myths.”

Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales, said Bennathan’s remarks were “hugely important” at the end of such a high-profile trial. “We’re pleased he emphasised and upheld women’s rights and freedoms, and recognised the profound courage of the women who came forward, and what they endured during the trial, too,” she said.

“This recognition stands in stark contrast to the appalling accusations made by Brand’s defence barrister, who perpetuated myths, misconceptions and conceptions about rape, such as needing to have fought, screamed or reported immediately for it to be considered a credible allegation. Of course this is not the case; there are a range of ways in which people respond to the threat of an imminent sexual assault and all of them are valid.”

Deniz Uğur, the deputy director of the End Violence Against Women Coalition, said rape myths should be prohibited. “The judge’s comments are welcome given the significant role that rape myths played in this trial, which in turn have influenced public discussions about the case,” she said. “This will be having a profound effect not only on the women involved in this case, but on survivors exposed to victim-blaming and misconceptions online and in their daily lives.”

On Tuesday, Labour’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, praised Bennathan’s “incredibly powerful” sentencing remarks, contrasting them with the “depressing” nature of the cross-examination of Brand’s victims by his barrister, Ian Winter KC.

The judge also took aim at Brand’s “enablers” who witnessed Brand sexually assault women in front of them at a radio station and TV studio. He said of the former incident: “No doubt your companions thought it was outrageous laddish behaviour that only you could get away with. It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offence, and as it turns out you haven’t got away with it.”

Bennathan told Brand the assault at the TV studio showed “your staggering arrogance, and it shows how your entourage indulged your dreadful behaviour”.

Bergman described the comments as “crucial”, adding: “This case and the national response to it is about more than just one man, it is about everyone who laughed along, didn’t speak up and/or looked away, even when it was happening right in front of them. They may not have committed Brand’s crimes, but they contributed to the culture that meant he went on harming other women with impunity for so long.”

Uğur similarly welcomed Bennathan’s remarks, saying it was “critically important to look at the many institutions and individuals that enabled [Brand’s] behaviour”.

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: Woman jailed for posing as man to dupe partner into sex found guilty of similar deception
excerpt:
Jury finds Blade Silvano, who presented herself as a male army veteran, guilty of six counts of sexual assault

A woman serving a prison sentence for sexual assault after pretending to be a man and du...
body_text:
Jury finds Blade Silvano, who presented herself as a male army veteran, guilty of six counts of sexual assault

A woman serving a prison sentence for sexual assault after pretending to be a man and duping a woman into a physical relationship has been found guilty of tricking another woman into a similar abusive partnership.

In both cases, Blade Silvano, 44, met the women on an online dating site and falsely claimed she was a man who had served in the armed forces before meeting them in person and sexually assaulting them.

Both women said Silvano tricked them into believing she was male and neither had any idea they were being deceived.

Silvano was jailed in 2023 in Cambridge after a jury heard she carried out the deception using a blindfold, sex toy and a “wholly fake persona”. Silvano and her victim even became engaged as a man and woman.

On Tuesday, a jury at Caernarfon crown court in north Wales found her guilty of six counts of sexual assault by penetration between November 2022 and the following June after being told she had carried out the same sort of deception on another woman.

Using the alias “Hunter”, Silvano began messaging the victim on the Plenty of Fish site before meeting her for sex, always keeping the lights very low and not allowing herself to be touched intimately.

Silvano claimed to be a captain and surgeon in the army and on one occasion claimed “his” condom had broken as they had sex. Silvano assured the alleged victim it was “very unlikely” she would get pregnant and told her: “Trust me, I’m a doctor.”

The jury was told the woman noticed her partner sounded a “little feminine” and began to have doubts about their “odd” sex life.

Eventually, the victim received a call from Silvano’s long-term partner, a woman, who said the person she’d known as “Hunter” was female, the court heard.

The victim told police she felt sick when she learned of the deception, saying: “I thought it was some sort of joke.” In court, she said: “I believed I was in a relationship with a straight, heterosexual man. I would never go out with a woman.”

Philip Clemo, prosecuting, told the jury Silvano was a gifted con artist and suggested she was inspired by the myth of Zeus turning into a bull.

The Cambridgeshire offences took place in 2016 and 2017. Using the fake name Blade Mendez, Silvano presented herself as a male army veteran throughout a two-year relationship.

She would send the victim photos of herself apparently shaving her face and would pretend to urinate standing up.

Silvano, of Shropshire, would not allow the victim to touch her genitals, claiming to be “body conscious due to injuries sustained in the army”. Silvano and the woman got engaged and she was encouraged to try on wedding dresses and book a registrar.

The victim accidentally uncovered Silvano’s deception after coming across her on Facebook in September 2018 “in a completely different living situation”. Silvano was found guilty of two counts of assault by penetration.

Silvano will be sentenced for the six sexual assaults next month. Judge Jones ordered a pre-sentence report so that the risk she posed could be assessed.
