title: Popular cooking methods may destroy key health benefits of broccoli, experts warn
excerpt: Cooking broccoli at high temperatures may reduce certain nutrients, but experts say a few easy kitchen adjustments, including adding mustard powder, could help retain more of the vegetable's beneficia...
body_text:
Cooking broccoli at high temperatures may reduce certain nutrients, but experts say a few easy kitchen adjustments, including adding mustard powder, could help retain more of the vegetable's beneficial properties.

Not all methods of cooking broccoli are created equal, and some simple tips can ensure you get the most nutrients out of it.

Whether it's steamed, roasted or added to a stir-fry, broccoli is a healthy option packed with vitamins such as A, C and K, minerals such as calcium, potassium and iron, fiber and even a potentially cancer-fighting compound, the Washington Post recently reported.

But certain ways of cooking broccoli can ensure you get the most out of the cruciferous vegetable and preserve those compounds.

YOU'RE PROBABLY COOKING RICE WRONG, AND CHEFS REVEAL THE SIMPLE MISTAKE TO AVOID

Boiling broccoli can cause water-soluble nutrients and compounds to leach into the cooking water, while prolonged or high-heat cooking, including roasting, can reduce antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and cancer-fighting properties.

Cruciferous vegetables provide fiber, vitamins and plant compounds being studied for potential health benefits. (iStock)

"Boiling causes the most loss in nutrients," Sol Figueroa, a Florida-based registered dietitian nutritionist with Mochi Health, told Fox News Digital. "Vitamin C and glucoraphanin dissolve in water, so a lot of them end up in the cooking water that gets poured down the drain."

NATURAL COMPOUND IN BLUEBERRIES AND GRAPES MAY UNLOCK FAT-BURNING PROCESS IN MUSCLE CELLS

Glucoraphanin is a natural compound found in cruciferous vegetables and, when it is digested, it can be converted into sulforaphane, a compound studied for potential antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects and possible benefits for liver, metabolic and gut health, as well as cancer prevention.

Figueroa offered several tips to help get the most out of your broccoli. One way to preserve some of the nutrients is to use as little water as possible when boiling, she said.

Chopping broccoli and letting it rest before cooking may give sulforaphane, a plant compound studied for potential health benefits, time to form. (iStock)

Another is to sprinkle mustard powder on cooked broccoli. Mustard seeds contain myrosinase, an enzyme that helps convert glucoraphanin to sulforaphane and that can be lost during cooking.

COMMON GRILLING MISTAKE COULD STRIP FISH OF KEY NUTRIENTS AND RUIN YOUR MEAL, EXPERTS WARN

Some simple prep also may help preserve sulforaphane, according to Figueroa.

"We can't say broccoli prevents disease, but the findings are promising."

"Chopping the broccoli and letting it sit for about 30 to 40 minutes before cooking gives sulforaphane time to form first," she said.

FOUR COMMON KITCHEN HABITS THAT CHEFS SAY HOME COOKS NEED TO STOP DOING IMMEDIATELY

Most of the research related to broccoli's health claims has been conducted in labs and animals, Figueroa added.

"We can't say broccoli prevents disease, but the findings are promising," she said.

Broccoli stalks are edible and can be trimmed, sliced and cooked alongside the florets. (iStock)

Steaming is one of the best ways to preserve broccoli's enzymes, and while the method often reduces vitamin C in other foods, research shows broccoli might be an exception, the Washington Post reported.

Quickly microwaving broccoli may help preserve nutrients, according to the outlet, and using broccoli's cooking water in soup or stew can help retain some water-soluble vitamins.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Felice Kaufman, a Florida-based food blogger at Cooking in the Keys and former New York Whole Foods Market chef, said she usually steams broccoli, cutting the florets into similar sizes and checking for doneness after about three minutes.

Steaming broccoli briefly may help preserve nutrients and compounds that can be reduced by prolonged cooking. (iStock)

"Taste a piece. If you'd eat it right then, take it out of the pot," Kaufman told Fox News Digital. "The heat keeps cooking the broccoli after it comes out of the pot."

Kaufman also recommends using the stalk, which she trims, slices and cooks with the florets.

She prefers steaming to boiling, in part to preserve vitamin C, but said that's not always possible.

"If the sink is full — it happens — I'll throw the broccoli straight into the boiling water," she said. "One less thing to wash."

Experts say the most important thing is to eat broccoli, whether it's steamed, roasted or prepared another way. (iStock)

No matter how it's served, getting some broccoli into your diet is key, experts agree.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The most important thing is eating broccoli at all," Figueroa said.

If roasting is the way your family likes it best, do that, she added.

Kaufman echoed that advice, saying, "Five ounces of broccoli, organic, conventional or frozen, is better than any processed food you can eat."

Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Disgraced former leader Sheikh Hasina plans return to Bangladesh from exile
excerpt:
Former prime minister faces death penalty upon return after being sentenced in absentia over deaths in 2024 uprising

Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according ...
body_text:
Former prime minister faces death penalty upon return after being sentenced in absentia over deaths in 2024 uprising

Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister of Bangladesh applied for a new passport this week.

Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She crossed the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.

Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.

Her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.

Hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had already returned in anticipation.

On Monday, a British lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina wrote to the Bangladesh high commission in Delhi requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.

“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.

Hasina has rejected the charges against her and claimed the tribunal that convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” said the Awami League leader.

Since Hasina’s conviction, the Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government, which was close to Hasina while she was in power, has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.

This week, the Bangladesh government said that, as a “terrorist”, Hasina would only be allowed to return via an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty.

Aminul Islam, the chief prosecutor of the tribunal that sentenced Hasina, said there was “no legal scope” for her to be issued a new passport as she was a “convicted fugitive”.

Islam emphasised that Hasina would be hanged if she returned, as the deadline for her to appeal against her conviction had passed. “Sheikh Hasina has no option but to face the execution of the verdict,” he said.

Despite her conviction and the party’s ban, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many of whom have been driven underground.

Analysts said they believed her decision to return was driven by an attempt to revive her support base and destabilise the newly elected government, led by Tarique Rahman. It came to power in February during Bangladesh’s first democratic election in decades.

The government has since struggled with inflation and protests that shut down garment factories, which the Awami League hopes to use to its advantage.

Another Awami League leader said all those in exile intended to follow Hasina back to Bangladesh, despite many of them facing serious criminal charges and having been given lengthy prison sentences in absentia.

“Some of us have been sentenced in absentia by kangaroo courts, and we know we will be jailed. But we are ready to face the consequences and return to our own people. We will fight this politically,” said the senior leader, who is based in India.

Some senior party figures have returned in recent months, including the former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. He was immediately arrested on his return in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder during the 2024 uprising.

Exiled Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.

Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press: “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people.”

title: France summons Iran’s ambassador over supermarket fridge ‘sabotage’
excerpt:
France says it has summoned Iran’s ambassador to Paris “to lodge a very strong protest” after it accused Tehran of carrying out a major cyberattack targeting supermarket fridges last month.

“It marks...
body_text:
France says it has summoned Iran’s ambassador to Paris “to lodge a very strong protest” after it accused Tehran of carrying out a major cyberattack targeting supermarket fridges last month.

“It marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation’s interests and the security of the French people,” Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Tuesday.

“I can also tell you that we rule nothing out and will take all measures – including those we may not disclose publicly – that we deem proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks,” he added.

Barrot, speaking on France Info ‌‌television, said the government would push for European Union sanctions in response to what he called an “attack of unprecedented scale and aggression in our country”.

He said firm measures would be taken “to deter anyone who might be tempted, in Iran or elsewhere, to do it again”.

On Monday, Barrot said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was behind cyberattacks targeting more than 700 French supermarkets on October 11 and 12, when refrigerators were remotely accessed “to initiate abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles”.

Raised temperatures in fridges forced the supermarkets to throw away all perishable food.

Millions of euros’ worth of food was spoiled, according to retailers. In some cases, the raised temperatures sparked fires or melted equipment.

French supermarket groups E-Leclerc, Intermarche, Carrefour, Monoprix and Cooperative U were all hit.

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said on Monday she had opened an investigation into Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit of the IRGC, over the attacks.

The prosecutor’s office has requested international arrest warrants be issued for two Shahid Kaveh officials.

Similar incidents have since been reported in other European countries.

In a suspected cyberattack on November 2, temperature spikes were recorded in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden.

Jody Westby, chief executive of Global Cyber Risk LLC, said tracking down the group directly responsible for the attacks is “very difficult” because of poor cooperation on international cybercrime investigations.

“It’s been a problem for 20 some years, and now it’s a little better, but only marginally so,” Westby told Al Jazeera. She said that it was difficult to track and trace the origin of such attacks “because of the nature of packet switching”.

In recent days, European air traffic has also been disrupted by false bomb alerts against dozens of flights, although the origin of those threats has yet to be determined.

title: Beau Lamarre-Condon denies stalking Jesse Baird as double murder trial continues
excerpt:
Former police officer tells jury he joked about being ‘white girl crazy’ with friends as lawyer questions him over start of relationship with Baird

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news...
body_text:
Former police officer tells jury he joked about being ‘white girl crazy’ with friends as lawyer questions him over start of relationship with Baird

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied being “obsessed” with Jesse Baird and stalking him, but admitted to following him online after their break up, a court has heard.

The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.

He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

Sitting in the witness box for the fourth day, Lamarre-Condon was shown screenshots he had taken of Baird’s Instagram story after their breakup in April 2023.

During his cross-examination on Tuesday, the crown prosecutor, Brett Hatfield SC, asked the former officer: “Were you stalking Jesse online and in person in this period in May and June 2023?”

Lamarre-Condon responded: “Mr Crown, if you’re going to accuse me of stalking you’re going to have to show my phone records of where I was on these dates.”

“I definitely wasn’t stalking him, I was looking online,” he told the NSW supreme court.

Lamarre-Condon repeatedly said he was the one who initiated the split, and told the jury this first break up with Baird was “amicable”.

“We always followed each other,” he told the court. “That’s not stalking. Am I looking at what he posts? Am I a follower? Yes.”

But the court heard he was still upset about the breakup.

“Jesse and I had good times together,” he said. “I did miss that and I miss him as a friend as well, not just as a sexual partner.”

Earlier, the former officer told the jury about the early days of their relationship, saying he met up with Baird in October and November 2022 for sexual encounters before the pair began going on romantic dates in December of that year.

Hatfield asked Lamarre-Condon: “You were obsessed with him right from the start?”

Lamarre-Condon denied this, telling the jury: “I never cared about showing Jesse off. I wanted Jesse to meet my friends because I thought he was genuine.

“Jesse Baird could have been a garbage cleaner … I liked Jesse for who he was as a person.”

Hatfield then asked if Lamarre-Condon was “obsessed” with Baird in February and March 2023, the accused responded: “I don’t agree with ‘obsessed’. Smitten? Yes. Obsessed? No.”

Hatfield pointed to messages between Lamarre-Condon and his friends sent around the time the pair began going on dates, where the officer says: “it sounds crazy, I love him.”

Lamarre-Condon responded: “I say ‘I love you’ to all my friends and to people like that all the time.

“That’s different to saying I’m ‘in’ love with him,” he said.

Asked whether he was insecure about the relationship and whether Baird liked him, Lamarre-Condon said his response was “natural” and sometimes occurred when the TV presenter did not reply to his messages straight away.

“I would always joke [with my friends], ‘we’re white girl crazy’,” Lamarre-Condon told the jury.

“It means we should stop being in our head and second-guessing ourselves.”

He told the court he would make jokes and have “banter” with his female friends, not his heterosexual male friends, telling each other things like: “You’re a crazy bitch.”

Lamarre-Condon told the court he had looked through Baird’s phone and used it to unfollow people when the pair went on a brief holiday to a cabin in regional NSW.

“In relation to breaching his privacy and, yes, his trust, I did unfollow two to three people,” he said.

“I believe curiosity just got the best of me.

“Our relationship was progressing, I just kind of wanted to see where he was at … if he was also messaging other guys romantically … I’m not making excuses for my behaviour.”

Later, when the prosecution attempted to go through messages between Lamarre-Condon and one of his friends, the officer directly addressed Hatfield, telling him: “Mr Crown, I think you’re trying to mislead me here.”

Justice Natalie Adams interjected, telling Lamarre-Condon to “just answer the question”.

“If the crown is misleading you, [the defence lawyer] will object,” she said.

title: California voters fail to pass proposed one-time tax on billionaires’ wealth
excerpt:
Campaign over Prop 40, as measure was known, was most expensive in state history, flush with Silicon Valley dollars

California billionaires won a contentious ballot measure campaign, defeating a prop...
body_text:
Campaign over Prop 40, as measure was known, was most expensive in state history, flush with Silicon Valley dollars

California billionaires won a contentious ballot measure campaign, defeating a proposed one-time tax on their wealth.

The bruising campaign over Proposition 40 was the most expensive in state history and witness to back-and-forth dealing from tech billionaires and democratic leaders, including Gavin Newsom, the governor, who steadfastly opposed the measure. While supporters of Prop 40 cast it as a solution to drastic healthcare cuts from Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, opponents led by prosperous billionaires mounted an influential campaign saying the billionaire tax was instead “an everyone tax”.

This result could hamper nationwide momentum on demands that billionaires pay their fair share and states enacting new laws to tax the ultra-wealthy.

Prop 40 proposed a one-time 5% tax on all individuals in California with a net worth of more than $1bn as of 1 January 2026. It was sponsored by the healthcare union SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, and dictated that the proceeds from the tax would fund healthcare programs, along with some education and food assistance.

The state’s major unions, and progressive politicians such as Bernie Sanders, the Vermont senator, and Ro Khanna, a California congressman, backed Prop 40. But both the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, as well as organizations such as Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, a lobbying branch of the healthcare group, opposed it – pointing to its structure as a one-off tax that would only fund certain healthcare programs. Prop 40’s most vocal critics, however, were the state’s billionaires.

Donors to the opposition campaign were a who’s who of Silicon Valley, including executives from Google, Palantir, DoorDash, Stripe and Reddit, along with several prominent venture capitalists. The biggest donor, by far, was Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder, who contributed at least $132m to fight the tax, according to campaign finance filings.

All told, the billionaires mounted a nearly $425m battle against Prop 40, making it the most expensive opposition campaign in state history. In the first two weeks of October, spending surpassed $2.5m a day, according to the most recent campaign finance filings.

Part of the opposition campaign’s strategy was mounting two separate counter-measures on the ballot, Proposition 41 and 42. Prop 41 directly targeted the billionaire tax, while Prop 42 was a general proposal on limiting certain new taxes and would ban any taxation on billionaire wealth. If either measure received more yes votes than Prop 40, they would stop the billionaire tax from taking effect – even if it passed.

Supporters of the billionaire tax called Props 41 and 42 “poison pills”.

title: Philadelphia Eagles hit rock bottom as coach Nick Sirianni denies flipping off home fans
excerpt: Dan reacts to former ESPN analyst Ryan Clark using his own messy Bristol firing to explain Troy Aikman’s looming exit, claiming the network is actively leaking negative stories to paint Aikman as the ...
body_text:
Dan reacts to former ESPN analyst Ryan Clark using his own messy Bristol firing to explain Troy Aikman’s looming exit, claiming the network is actively leaking negative stories to paint Aikman as the bad guy while shielding Joe Buck and executive leadership.

Things have gone completely off the rails in Philly.

The Philadelphia Eagles sit at 2-7, and Nick Sirianni is defending himself against accusations of giving Eagles fans the bird.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Sunday’s 19-11 divisional loss against the New York Giants was bad enough on its own. New York had not won in South Philly since 2013, and the loss marked seven straight for an Eagles squad in free fall.

EAGLES HEAD COACH SAYS HE'D NEED TO BE A BETTER ACTOR THAN JOEY TRIBBIANI TO TONE DOWN HIS BEHAVIOR

Right after the final whistle, cameras caught Sirianni walking off with security chief Big Dom, appearing to raise his right middle finger toward booing fans.

Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni looks on during the game against the New York Giants on Nov. 8, 2026, at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Pa. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Failing to stack up wins is one thing. Turning the home crowd into your enemy is the quickest way to get run out of town.

Asked about it Monday, Sirianni flatly denied flipping off the home fans.

"Absolutely not," Sirianni said. "That was a surprise to me. Absolutely not."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Sirianni has always been a loose cannon. Fans loved it when he was barking at road crowds in Kansas City and Indianapolis or jawing at opposing sidelines. He even caught flak for cupping his ear at the Linc during an ugly win over Cleveland. Taunting outside haters works when you're winning, but picking fights with paying hometown customers during a collapse is pure self-sabotage.

The offense is running on fumes without the retired Lane Johnson and with Jalen Hurts sidelined.

JALEN HURTS TO REPORTEDLY MISS REMAINDER OF NFL SEASON AFTER BLOOD CLOTS FOUND IN QUARTERBACK'S LUNGS

Interim starting Eagles QB Joe Milton had an expectedly ugly afternoon, throwing 18-of-34 for 169 yards, coughing up a lost fumble, and taking seven sacks, including three from Giants rookie linebacker Arvell Reese.

Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni reacts against the Chicago Bears during the second quarter at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Pa., on Nov. 28, 2025. (Getty Images)

Across the field, a physical, Harbaugh-led Giants squad looks ready to take the NFC East. New York rotated J.J. McCarthy on the ground to move the chains and let Jameis Winston punch in the go-ahead score.

GIANTS STAR WIDEOUT BLASTS ANALYST FOR QUESTIONING SIDELINE BEHAVIOR DURING WIN AGAINST EAGLES

Head coach Nick Sirianni of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on during the second quarter against the Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium on Nov. 1, 2026, in Landover, Md. (Getty Images)

In the aftermath of the loss, Eagles general manager Howie Roseman hit the fire-sale button, trading defensive tackle Jordan Davis to Jacksonville on Monday for first and second-round picks. Philadelphia now holds 10 selections in the top two rounds over the next three drafts.

The future draft capital is loaded for tomorrow, but the present state of the Eagles is a complete disaster.

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

title: Harare demolitions leave families homeless after years of building
excerpt: Harare, Zimbabwe – At around 5am on Friday, August 14, Methro Masunga, 28, was jolted awake by the sound of bulldozers and shouting municipal police officers. Outside, earth-moving vehicles were prepa...
body_text:
Harare, Zimbabwe – At around 5am on Friday, August 14, Methro Masunga, 28, was jolted awake by the sound of bulldozers and shouting municipal police officers. Outside, earth-moving vehicles were preparing to demolish homes in St Martins Extension, a suburb of Harare.

At first, Masunga thought the machinery had arrived for roadworks. Then she realised her home was among those marked for destruction.

“I thought they were here for some other business, probably land development or road grading; alas, they had been sent to destroy our homes. We tried to understand, but no one would hear us,” Masunga told Al Jazeera.

A single mother of three, Masunga had spent years saving to own a home. She worked part-time cleaning other people’s houses, putting aside what she could to buy a residential stand.

“I worked part-time jobs doing laundry and washing dishes in people’s houses for five years, saving where possible. So, when I came here, I paid the deposit and started monthly contributions,” she said, standing among the remains of her house.

Masunga began paying for her stand in 2015 and received an allocation in 2019. She says the arrangement was formalised through the city council in 2020, when residents began receiving official documents.

Her experience reflects a wider dispute over land allocations in Harare. Residents say they bought stands through council-linked processes and invested their savings in building homes. The municipality says it is enforcing planning regulations against structures built without the necessary approvals or on land not designated for housing.

The full number of people displaced by demolitions across Harare in 2026 has not been independently established. However, city council records seen by Al Jazeera list more than 5,000 houses facing demolition under 37 outstanding High Court orders. These figures concern properties targeted under the wider programme, not homes already demolished. A council task force has separately inspected 22,255 sites to identify structures on prohibited or unauthorised land.

Authorities say the demolitions are intended to address illegal construction, disputed land sales and development on sites reserved for public infrastructure. Residents argue that enforcement has also affected people who say they obtained allocation letters and agreements of sale through municipal processes.

Memory Chengeta, whose house in St Martins was also demolished, said residents were bewildered by the operation because of an earlier court order.

“There was a court order for them to stop demolitions. The municipal authorities came with no court order that overturned the previous judgement, but went ahead to destroy the properties,” she said.

A former street food vendor, Chengeta had saved to build a more stable life. She is now homeless. Some affected residents have returned to renting, while others, including Chengeta and Masunga, have remained in St Martins, putting up makeshift shelters rather than leaving the area.

Joachim Nhete also lost his home after using his retirement package to buy land and build a house. He estimates his investment at more than $10,000.

The dispute has raised questions about how residents acquired their stands and whether the council complied with existing court orders.

On October 29, 2025, Justice Happias Zhou issued a consent order in case HCH5444/25, setting aside demolition notices issued to named applicants in St Martins Extension. It barred the City of Harare from evicting those applicants or demolishing their homes without a valid court order. It also prohibited further development without written council approval.

The order did not automatically protect every property in St Martins. The available information does not establish whether Masunga, Chengeta or their specific properties were among those covered.

The council has maintained that it did not demolish properties protected by the order. Its spokesperson, Stanley Gama, told local media that the municipality was targeting structures whose owners had repeatedly been warned against building illegally.

“We are only demolishing structures built illegally whose owners were told and warned many times not to proceed with construction,” Gama said.

Harare Mayor Jacob Mafume told NewsDay on August 15 that residents with approved building plans should produce them during council inspections. He said the municipality had repeatedly warned residents to obtain the necessary documents but declined to comment on the legality of the specific demolitions in St Martins.

Harare’s principal housing director, Edgar Dzehonye, later said residents had been warned against building in the area because it had not been adequately serviced.

These explanations raise a separate question: whether residents who received council allocation letters and agreements of sale also had valid planning and building approvals. An allocation to occupy a stand does not necessarily establish that a house was authorised for construction. The status of the residents’ documents, the approved layout, and individual building permits are therefore central to determining whether the demolitions were justified.

Precious Shumba, director of the Harare Residents’ Trust, said the demolitions were particularly troubling because of the court order protecting residents allocated stands by the municipality.

“Despite that, the town planning department and legal officers in the Chamber Secretary’s Department issued directives to the Municipal Police to demolish the houses of St Martins Extension residents,” he said.

Zimbabwe’s Constitution, under Section 74, prohibits the eviction of people from their homes or the demolition of their homes without a court order made after considering all relevant circumstances. The National Human Settlements Policy also calls for alternative accommodation to be prepared before relocations and demolitions. Residents say they were not offered alternative housing.

The controversy reflects long-standing problems in Harare’s land administration. A 2019 commission of inquiry chaired by Justice Tendai Uchena identified unauthorised land sales, weak administration and poor record-keeping by local authorities. It found that land barons had sold state land without authority, sometimes allegedly working alongside council officials.

Shumba said the Harare Residents’ Trust wrote to the president on July 22, 2026, calling for the publication of the report of the commission of inquiry into the financial affairs of the city of Harare. The organisation also wants the findings of the Justice Maphios Cheda commission of inquiry into the city’s governance crisis implemented.

David Jenje, chairman of the St Martins Residents Association and the St Martins Housing Happiness Pay Scheme, said residents had paid for their stands years before receiving allocation letters.

He said the council’s Education, Housing and Community Services Committee resolved in 2019 to expedite the allocation and servicing of the land.

“Most of the members had paid deposits of $5,000 as far back as 2018 … Allocations were made in July 2019 after completion of payment of intrinsic land value. All the allocation letters and agreements of sale were signed in February 2020. These demolitions were illegal,” Jenje said.

ZimRights, a human rights organisation, said the demolitions raised questions about the rule of law and accountability.

Harare South MP Trymore Kanopula called for a halt to further demolitions until the land allocations had been audited and investigated. He also urged the government to present the findings of the commission of inquiry into state land sales to Parliament.

Parliament’s speaker referred the matter to the Ministry of Local Government and Public Works for action.

Minister Daniel Garwe said the government did not carry out demolitions and could not interfere with court processes. He acknowledged that the Harare City Council had approximately 5,000 demolition orders and said the government had sometimes tried to delay demolitions while seeking solutions.

For Nhete, however, official interventions offer little comfort. His house is gone, and he says he has no insurance to recover his investment.

“Unlike some who had home insurance, I didn’t have one,” he said. “I cannot recover the loss and pain. My hope is in the courts of law that Harare City Council must be held accountable and pay us back.”

title: Russia, Ukraine and US to meet as Zelenskyy claims battlefield successes
excerpt: Negotiators from Russia and Ukraine are set to meet for peace talks brokered by the United States in Abu Dhabi, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying that recent gains on the battlefield...
body_text:
Negotiators from Russia and Ukraine are set to meet for peace talks brokered by the United States in Abu Dhabi, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying that recent gains on the battlefield had strengthened his country’s hand.

The meeting in the capital of the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday will be the third round of talks there this year, following security consultations in January and February. The US side is led by US President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have spearheaded Washington’s mediation.

The three delegations last met in Geneva on February 18.

“Ukrainian forces are currently genuinely strengthening Ukraine’s negotiating position,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address on Monday. He said Russia was “suffering record losses”, a claim Moscow disputes, and urged Washington to persuade the Kremlin to end the war.

Zelenskyy said General Mykhailo Drapatyi had presented a report on Ukraine’s military positions that pointed to heavy recent Russian losses, and that Ukraine’s long-range strikes on targets inside Russia, including oil facilities, were having an effect.

“We are responding to Russia’s war in a fully justified manner and demonstrating that this war must end,” he said. “Russia can do this. It can end its war. It is important that the United States convince Russia of precisely this.”

In Washington, DC, Trump told reporters that he saw a “very strong inclination” towards ending the war and that both sides were “tired of fighting”.

“We’re having a very good conversation about that in Abu Dhabi,” he said.

Trump had promised to end the war quickly when he took office in January 2025, but a settlement has remained elusive nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

A US official, briefing reporters on the condition of anonymity, said on Monday that both Russia and Ukraine had privately shown some flexibility on a possible exchange of territory. Security guarantees for Ukraine would be a central topic, the official said, including the possibility of a defence commitment modelled on Article 5 of NATO’s founding treaty.

Both Ukraine and Russia have been adamant about territory.

Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to obtain all of the Donbas region.

Russia occupies roughly 20 percent of Ukraine, including Crimea and parts of the eastern Donbas region. The Russian move has not been recognised by the international community, but Trump has previously urged Kyiv to cede territory for a deal to end the war.

The US official said any territorial agreement would most likely come at the end of the negotiations, once other issues, including a post-war security framework, had been settled.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio meanwhile struck a cautious note, saying that the process to end the war still has “a ways to go”.

“We’ll keep trying. And that’s what we’ve been trying to do the whole time is try to be creative and find ways that we can help bring that conflict and that war to an end,” Rubio said.

Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, will again lead the country’s delegation, according to The Kyiv Independent. Russia’s team will be headed by Vladimir Medinsky, a Kremlin aide, and will include Sergei Ryabkov, a deputy foreign minister, as well as Yuri Zhigarlovsky, a senior military officer.

European powers, including France, Germany and the European Commission, will send officials to the talks in Abu Dhabi, but Russia has made it clear it doesn’t want the Europeans to take part in negotiations.

Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said the talks would focus on security guarantees. European officials would not take part, he added, because the negotiations had been agreed to as a three-way format.

“What will take place in Abu Dhabi in the coming days is trilateral negotiations between Russia and Ukraine with US mediation,” Peskov said. “As for the presence of Europeans, you know that the Americans have their own channels of communication with Europeans, and Ukrainians with Europeans.”

title: Australia to introduce mandatory reporting after OpenAI hack to combat artificial intelligence ‘going rogue’
excerpt:
Government flags criminal law changes to ensure companies can’t argue in future ‘that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded’

OpenAI won’t face criminal penalties over the Medicare hack but the ...
body_text:
Government flags criminal law changes to ensure companies can’t argue in future ‘that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded’

OpenAI won’t face criminal penalties over the Medicare hack but the prime minister has flagged changes to Australia’s criminal law to crack down on future breaches by artificial intelligence companies.

Anthony Albanese on Tuesday released the recommendations of a “rapid review” into the June breach but not the findings or the report itself.

A key recommendation is for the attorney general’s department, the Australian federal police and home affairs to consider reforming the law to introduce “penalties for egregious regulatory non-compliance” and a “failure to prevent” offence which would criminalise developing an AI model that engaged in harmful conduct while failing “to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm”.

The review recommended the federal government “consider mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting, including but not limited to misaligned behaviour or agentic cyber incidents”.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, told reporters “we need to make sure that our laws and our systems keep pace with the technology and also make sure that we’re able to use the technology to find vulnerabilities before others do”.

“The mandatory reporting, when artificial intelligence goes rogue, gives us a chance to be able to make sure that when this happens, the reporting occurs and occurs immediately,” Burke said in Canberra alongside the PM.

On the “concept of looking at how we can update our criminal law”, Burke said: “It should never be the case that there’s an argument that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded.”

“We need to make sure that the criminal law is up to date for how this new technology is able to act.”

Albanese on Tuesday characterised OpenAI’s breach of Services Australia as “minor” in terms of the implications for personal privacy.

“The clear indication is that no information was got that involves people’s personal details,” the prime minister told reporters in Canberra.

“All of that was confirmed essentially ... but that doesn’t mean that it wasn’t a serious issue and that in other areas there might be more serious implications.”

The review made 18 recommendations. Albanese said “we accept all of the recommendations and we’ve commenced work to implement them”.

Albanese did not directly answer a question about whether the OpenAI incident in June would have breached the proposed new laws if they were in place.

The AI agent developed by OpenAI accessed Services Australia data and three other systems in June.

The company didn’t notify the Australia government until mid-September despite becoming aware of the incident itself in August.

Guardian Australia revealed last month OpenAI used AI to help write the email to notify Australian authorities.

Albanese said the government would set up a new AI safety regulator.

Labor would consider six key obligations on AI companies, including:

maintaining security controls across all stages of development and deployment;

identify and manage serious risks associated with their models;

provide mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian government rapidly;

allow independent evaluation of their models;

maintain and publish safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management, and transparency;

and respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change.

title: College Football Playoff committee executive admits they don't care fans are against 24-team playoff
excerpt:
The College Football Playoffs are set to expand from 12 to 24 teams starting next season, and Craig Carton asked former Heisman trophy finalist and CFB analyst Ryan Leaf his take on the change.

Monda...
body_text:
The College Football Playoffs are set to expand from 12 to 24 teams starting next season, and Craig Carton asked former Heisman trophy finalist and CFB analyst Ryan Leaf his take on the change.

Monday made what was long rumored official: we're moving to a 24-team College Football Playoff starting in the 2027-2028 season.

The reaction from most fans, commentators, analysts as well as many coaches and people within the sport, can be summed up in one word: why?

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

As recently as 2023, the playoff was four teams. The smaller field ensured that the best of the best would compete for a title. Only one-loss or undefeated teams had a chance at postseason glory ... well, unless you were an undefeated Florida State team.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF EXPANDING TO 24 TEAMS IN 2027, WITH MORE GAMES COMING TO CAMPUSES ACROSS THE COUNTRY

SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey speaks during a roundtable discussion on college sports in the East Room of the White House on March 6, 2026, as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick looks on. The Trump administration hosted the event titled "Saving College Sports" with leaders from the Power Four conferences, media executives and former coaches. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Then, in 2024, we moved to a 12-team format, which offered more opportunity for teams to change their season. The 2024-2025 Ohio State Buckeyes were a perfect example, losing the final game of the season before roaring back to life and steamrolling their way through to a championship.

The 12-team format has generally been well liked; it's a solid balance of maintaining the exclusivity of the tournament, while adding more big postseason games on campuses and mostly preserving bowl season and the importance of the regular season. While the upcoming 2026-2027 version of the playoff will be just the third under the expanded format, we're already moving on to even more teams. Somehow.

24 teams essentially means the end of meaningful bowl games. With a bowl field so diluted by the increase in playoff participants, the remaining bowls will be picking up scraps. Major conference championship games are set to become a thing of the past.

The regular season, long the best in sports, will be significantly less meaningful. Not only will three losses not be enough to keep teams out, there's a strong chance that four or potentially even five loss teams (from the SEC) will be in the 24-team playoff. This might mean more scheduled games between big programs, since they'll no longer be concerned about a single loss hurting their chances, but if it doesn't, the sport will have sacrificed the regular season almost entirely.

Which again, raises the all-important question: who wanted this? Who was asking for it? Why is it even happening?

Big Ten Conference Commissioner Tony Petitti speaks during the 2025 Big Ten Football Media Days at Mandalay Bay Convention Center in Las Vegas, Nev., on July 22, 2025. (Louis Grasse/Getty Images)

The answer is money, money and money. The Big Ten led the charge for more playoff spots, and other conferences and groups eventually fell in line. The SEC, long the hold out, caved, presumably because commissioner Greg Sankey realized he could start campaigning for all 16 conference teams to reach the playoff each season.

Obviously, more playoff games means more money coming from the broadcast partner, ESPN. More teams will have late-season home games with a potential "playoff appearance" on the line. Then be able to sell expensive home playoff game tickets to their fans. Coaches now have a lower bar to claim a successful season. And boosters can see a return on investment instead of seeing their money go towards reaching the Pop-Tarts Bowl.

The one group missing here? Fans. As usual. Fans weren't asking for this, and surveys have shown that they overwhelmingly don't want it. Unsurprisingly, it's happening anyway. And in a news conference announcing the change, Executive Director Rich Clark explained why: the playoff committee doesn't care.

BIG TEN CONFERENCE COMMISSIONER GIVES TONE DEAF STATEMENT ABOUT 24-TEAM COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF

Clark said on the call that changes brought about by the 24-team field will be beneficial for the sport, and most importantly, the business school executive's new favorite word: "stakeholders."

"New scheduling standards will incentivize institutions to schedule more compelling non-conference matchups during the regular season, and 16 Playoff games will now be played on campuses, bringing Playoff football to more students and local fans," Clark said. "Finally, our commitment as the CFP administration and staff, we will make the 24-team Playoff spectacular for the fans, for the student-athletes, for the institutions, and for all our stakeholders."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Clark answered a few questions, saying that the committee will evaluate and encourage strong schedules, and teams will be required to play 10 games against teams from Power 4 conferences. title: Senate advances bill to speed up projects from gas pipelines to clean energy
excerpt:
Key environmental groups come out against bipartisan Baaja bill over fears it could spur datacenters and ICE jails

The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting...
body_text:
Key environmental groups come out against bipartisan Baaja bill over fears it could spur datacenters and ICE jails

The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for datacenters and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

It’s a bill that would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America – everything from fossil fuel pipelines to transmission lines that would add more clean energy to the grid. And it would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal. That is why climate advocates are torn over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs act (Baaja).

The Senate voted on Monday to open debate on Baaja in the first of several procedural votes. Senators voted 73-25 on the cloture motion, which did not result in the bill being passed, but pushed it another step forward.

Trump urged all senators to vote for the 417-page bill, which is sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats in the Senate, but after last week’s historic “blue wave” elections, some environmental and tribal advocates called on Democratic leadership to pump the brakes.

Earthjustice, the Sierra Club and the ACLU have come out against the bill because it would significantly weaken environmental laws including the National Environmental Policy Act (Nepa) and accelerate the construction of gas pipelines and ICE detention centers.

Indigenous groups held a press conference on Friday calling on senators to vote against Baaja because it would weaken the federal government’s legal obligation to consult tribes on projects that affect them.

“This is such an existential threat to Indian country,” said Mark Macarro, president of the National Congress of American Indians.

Protesters rallied outside Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer’s building on Friday over concerns that the bill could boost datacenters. “It would be highly ironic if, having won an election where datacenter opposition was at the front and center, the first act of Congress was to make it easier to build datacenters,” said Bill McKibben.

Democrats elected in the blue wave will not take their seats until January, so the bill’s proponents still have time to rush it through the Senate, and technically there is time for it to pass in the House before new Congress and go to Trump.

But midterm success for the Democrats is dialing up the political friction. House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, expected to be the House speaker in the new Congress, said the bill “falls short in several areas”, including failing to protect tribal sovereignty, and he would not “rubber-stamp legislation without more constructive involvement with our caucus”.

Earlier on Monday, the bill’s Democratic sponsors, Senators Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse, said they had the votes to pass the bill. Heinrich said they had made last-minute changes to ensure tribal consultation, and they believed the bill would favor renewables over fossil fuels. “If we can create an open, competitive level playing field, clean is cheap, and cheap wins in the marketplace,” Heinrich said.

Whitehouse, who wore a tie with wind turbines on it, argued that passing the bill would set the stage for Democrats to work on clean energy policies next year with majorities in the House and Senate. “People should just cool their jets and have a little faith that this is not the end of the story,” he said.

Proponents of Baaja say it is needed because it takes too long to build large projects in America and the bill shortens timelines. It simplifies federal rules for building interstate transmission lines, it narrows what gets reviewed under the National Historic Preservation Act and limits tribal consultation, it limits the use of the Clean Water Act, shortens timelines for the Endangered Species Act, limits how the executive branch can interfere with federal permitting, and makes big changes to Nepa such as changing what requires Nepa review and who has standing to sue.

The fossil fuel industry is backing Baaja. The American Petroleum Institute (API) hailed the bill as “a historic opportunity” and called on congress to “finish permitting reform this year”.

“It creates a very accelerated fast track for gas pipelines,” said Earthjustice Action’s president, Abbie Dillen. “The gas industry is extraordinarily excited about this because they are interested in expanding existing pipeline capacity to get more liquefied natural gas out for export, and to be feeding power-hungry datacenters with gas.”

The bill could help pave the way for the Constitution gas pipeline that Williams Companies is trying to build through New York. The state denied the project’s water quality permit in 2016, but the company has revived the project under the Trump administration. The proposed pipeline could benefit from the bill’s changes to the Clean Water Act.

Baaja could also enable construction of gas pipelines in the west. Fossil fuel advocacy group Western States and Tribal Nations wants to build gas pipelines to feed domestic datacenters and export LNG from the west coast. During a 3 November election day meeting with Wyoming’s Sweetwater county board of commissioners, the advocacy group’s president, Andrew Browning, said he was talking to lawmakers about the bill: “The permitting bill’s a huge thing … We’re going to need that for everything we’re envisioning and building out.”

Some clean energy advocates want the bill to pass because it would connect renewables to the grid. Wind, solar and battery storage are now cheap to build, but the country lacks the necessary transmission lines to bring clean energy where it’s needed.

Interstate transmission lines can take a decade to get built, and energy projects also face a bottleneck in connecting to the grid. At the end of 2025, 2,060 GW of total generation and storage capacity were waiting in a queue to connect to the grid.

Ben King, energy and climate director at Rhodium Group, said Baaja would reform the interconnection queue process and unlock the ability to build the transmission that is needed. “We’re at a pretty low point for policy support for clean [energy],” he said, referring to Trump’s repeal of clean energy tax credits. “[Baaja] sets up the ability to build stuff more quickly for when the next wave of climate policy happens.”

Many experts have modeled what the bill would do to emissions, but there is a lot of uncertainty on that question. Rhodium Group’s analysis found that domestic emissions go down if Baaja passes. But another model by the Purdue engineering professor Kevin Kircher found it would increase domestic emissions.

Kircher said the optimistic case for Baaja is that there’s a huge amount of clean energy ready to go, and if we get rid of the long queues and regulations, “level the playing field and let it rip”, then clean energy wins on the economics. “I think that understanding is outdated,” he said.

What the bill does to emissions partly depends on what type of energy gets connected to the grid. Rhodium Group assumed, based on a report from 2025, that 85% of the capacity added to the grid would be renewables. But Kircher said some grid operators have updated their queues this year to remove redundant and speculative offers. (PJM’s queue as of 3 August looks quite gassy.)

King said the economics show an impressive decrease in the cost of renewables, while fossil fuels are not getting any cheaper. “Some of it is just a bet on what’s going to win out in the future,” he said. “Our modeling suggests that clean stuff is going to dominate energy expansion for the foreseeable future, and there might be people who have a different view on that. API might have a different perspective – they might bet that there’s more room for them to grow.”

Kircher emphasized that the various models have not had time for peer review since the bill was first introduced on 30 September. “We need to have some humility in recognizing that the process of taking that 417 pages of super dense legal text and mapping it … is extremely complicated and full of uncertainties,” he said.

The bill would significantly reduce the scope of Nepa. It would narrow the definition of a “major federal action” that would trigger Nepa review, and effectively eliminate the authority of courts to enforce Nepa compliance.

Nepa is the powerful law that attorneys used to block the Trump administration’s plans to convert 11 mega-warehouses into massive ICE detention centers. If the bill passes, it could accelerate the development of ICE detention centers, according to a letter the American Civil Liberties Union sent to senators. “As written, this bill would hamper, if not altogether thwart, critical work by the ACLU and our partners to halt ICE’s dangerous expansion of immigrant detention,” the letter said.

Baaja’s passage would be “the single biggest overhaul” of American environmental laws since the 1970s, said Dillen of Earthjustice. “There are legitimate concerns that Nepa has been weaponized to slow down important projects, but people have recognized this problem for years, and the law has been reformed, and it’s also been weakened very significantly by the supreme court. What this bill does is take the last pieces of it that are very relevant in an administration like this,” she said.

Trump has pushed a “drill, baby, drill” fossil fuel agenda, and Baaja’s weakening of environmental regulations would further embolden him, Dillen said. She pointed to Trump’s plan to allow drilling near Chaco Culture national historic park, a Unesco world heritage site. “Chaco Canyon is in the crosshairs,” she said.

“At Earthjustice, we are deeply committed to building clean energy and to do it in a time frame that is meaningful, given the threats that we face. But the way to do this, the way to build our country better and even faster, is not by running over tribes and by emboldening a president who voters have just come out in a historic turnout to push back on,” Dillen said.

title: Police investigate as nearly 30 Santa Barbara half-marathon runners fall ill with ‘unusual symptoms’
excerpt:
Runners seek medical treatment as 13-mile race held amid unusually high November temperatures

Police in southern California are investigating the circumstances that led to the hospitalization of near...
body_text:
Runners seek medical treatment as 13-mile race held amid unusually high November temperatures

Police in southern California are investigating the circumstances that led to the hospitalization of nearly 30 runners who participated in the Santa Barbara Half on Sunday.

Santa Barbara police said in a statement to the Associated Press that they had opened an investigation after receiving reports from Santa Barbara Cottage Hospital about multiple half-marathon participants seeking medical treatment for “unusual symptoms”.

Cottage Health said in a statement it had a “larger than expected number of emergency visits … a number of them with similar symptoms of undetermined cause”.

Race organizers say they believe any illness is attributable to heat or dehydration. The high on the day of the race was 88F (31.1C), an unusually high temperature for this time of year.

Neither the hospital nor police have detailed the symptoms beyond calling them unusual. Cottage Health said on Monday that 27 participants came to emergency rooms in Santa Barbara and Goleta, a small city about 10 miles west.

More than 4,640 people competed in the half-marathon, which spanned about 13 miles, according to the Santa Barbara Half Marathon website.

Of those who were either taken to the hospital or arrived there on their own, 24 patients had been treated and discharged as of Monday morning. The three others were in stable condition, the company told the Associated Press.

Event director David Monico said organizers transported 15 people from the medical tent to local hospitals. He said the event’s medical team treated numerous runners for dehydration and overheating both on the course and at the finish line.

The half-marathon’s event director, David Monico told the Guardian that they have “no additional information to suggest that the issues some of the participants experienced were caused by anything other than endurance event exertion-related symptoms”.

title: Todd Russell, Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor, dies aged 54 due to illness
excerpt:
Tasmanian premier leads tributes for Russell, who earlier this month returned home to ‘see out his days’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beaconsfield mine collapse surviv...
body_text:
Tasmanian premier leads tributes for Russell, who earlier this month returned home to ‘see out his days’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor Todd Russell has died aged 54 after recently announcing deteriorating health.

The Tasmanian premier, Jeremy Rockliff, led the tributes on Tuesday morning, saying his thoughts were with Russell’s loved ones.

“Vale Todd Russell,” Rockliff wrote on social media.

“Thoughts this morning are with Todd’s loved ones and everyone who had the absolute pleasure of knowing him.”

The disaster sparked global headlines and became a rallying event for the nation in 2006 after a minor earthquake sparked a collapse at the Beaconsfield goldmine.

The event killed miner Larry Knight, with fears Russell and his co-worker, Brant Webb, were also entombed by thousands of tonnes of rock and debris.

The pair were initially presumed dead before their faint cries were heard by searching workmates days later.

Rescuers used thermal imaging cameras and found the pair alive five days after the collapse, trapped in a safety cage almost a kilometre down.

The men had survived on a shared cereal bar and water that seeped through the rock, before meals were able to be passed down to them through a pipe.

A major technical rescue effort to free the pair was launched, and they ultimately walked free after two weeks underground, throwing their hands into the air before embracing their loved ones.

The disaster left a deep mark on Australia’s cultural fabric, and it was the subject of the 2007 Foo Fighters song Ballad of the Beaconsfield Miners.

Russell told the ABC’s I Was Actually There podcast in 2024 he had struggled with his mental health and relationships after the disaster, saying he had developed PTSD.

“I needed a reality check, which [my then wife] Carolyn gave me, to go and seek the help that I needed from the right people [about] the PTSD and the depression,” he said at the time. “There are days that are good days, there’s days that are bad days and there’s days that trigger little things.

“I’m continuously trying to rebuild that relationship [with my kids]. I’ve got a one-year-old granddaughter. She’s absolutely beautiful, so I’ve got that to focus on now.”

In 2025, Russell announced he had started treatment in hospital for an undisclosed illness.

Earlier in November, he announced he would return home to “see out his days” with friends and family.

“After years of pain, uncertainty, appointments, treatments, setbacks, and endless battles, plus the emotional exhaustion of having to pick myself up time and time again, have left me with nothing left to give,” he posted on social media.

Speaking to ABC, Webb said his thoughts were with his friend’s family.

“Twenty years ago, Todd and I, we experienced something that probably most other people don’t experience,” he said.

“Being trapped and thinking you are going to die... it brought us very close.

“One thing we had in common was that we both had kids... and you know you only get one dad, and yeah, they’d be really hurting today.”

The Beaconsfield disaster was “two weeks that stopped a nation,” Rockliff wrote on social media on Tuesday. “But Todd didn’t let it define him. He continued to serve proudly at the Beaconsfield fire brigade until February this year, an exemplary 31-year career of community service.”

Beaconsfield Fire Brigade thanked Russell for his years of service as a brigade chief.

“Todd dedicated his time and service to the brigade and the community, leaving behind a legacy that will be remembered by those who had the privilege of serving alongside him,” the brigade wrote on social media.

Rockliff also praised Russell for sharing his mental health struggle.

“He told his story, and became an advocate for mental health,” the premier wrote, “and made the community around him a better place.”

Close friend and Tasmanian Liberal MP Michael Ferguson described getting to know Russell as an honour.

“Todd has endured so much over these past few years,” he wrote on Facebook.

Ferguson recalled seeing Russell in good spirits as recently as Friday, saying the former miner was thrilled to have returned home.

“My heart goes out to Todd and his family as they spend this precious time together,” he said.

“I promised him I would keep praying for him.”

title: NTSB recovers cockpit voice recorder from Learjet crash site in Florida
excerpt: Retired Navy fighter pilot Matthew 'Whiz' Buckley discusses the aircraft's damaged tail components, rapid descent and encounter with severe weather, as investigators work to determine what caused the ...
body_text:
Retired Navy fighter pilot Matthew 'Whiz' Buckley discusses the aircraft's damaged tail components, rapid descent and encounter with severe weather, as investigators work to determine what caused the deadly Florida Learjet crash.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) announced on Monday that it has recovered the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) of the Learjet 60 that crashed last week near Greenacres, Florida, killing all nine people on board.

"NTSB investigators have recovered the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) of the Learjet 60 that crashed on Nov. 1 near Greenacres, Florida," the NTSB said on X.

The CVR was found at the location of the initial impact​, according to the NTSB.

The NTSB said the CVR is being evaluated in the board's Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C.

TIMELINE OF LEARJET CRASH THAT KILLED AUSTIN FAMILY TRACES FINAL MINUTES FROM TAKEOFF TO FLORIDA PLUNGE

NTSB investigators recovered the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) of the Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida. (NTSB)

The excavation work at the impact site has been completed.

This comes after investigators said on Friday that they recovered part of an engine from the Learjet.

Crews started excavating the site on Wednesday after utility workers had drained water and cleared other hazards, the NTSB said.

Once investigators began digging, they found a part of one engine, the board said.

Earlier last week, investigators recovered the left tail elevator, which controls the jet's pitch, in three separate pieces. One of them was found nearly four miles from where the Learjet 60 crashed.

FLORIDA PLANE CRASH VICTIMS IDENTIFIED AFTER 9 PEOPLE KILLED IN FIERY WRECK

The cockpit voice recorder was found at the location of initial impact and is being evaluated in the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C. (NTSB)

"Even small pieces of the wreckage may contain important evidence that could help investigators determine what happened," the agency wrote last week on X.

The Learjet 60 left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport around 10:37 a.m. on Sunday, bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas. The aircraft plunged into the ground in Palm Beach County shortly before 1 p.m., killing everyone aboard.

Austin tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, 45, was killed in the crash alongside his wife, Helen Sharp, 40, their children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, the children's nanny, Anita Maria Cetina, and couple Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr.

Heavy rain and thunderstorms were reported across South Florida when the Learjet crashed. Investigators said the weather will be a major focus of their probe.

Investigators work at the scene of a plane crash in Greenacres, Florida, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)

At about 41,000 feet, an air traffic controller told the flight crew that moderate precipitation was roughly five miles away and said they could move either left or right, stressing that the turn toward Freeport in the Bahamas "looks pretty bad."

The crew was then instructed to fly to a waypoint near Naples, Florida. The crew made a deviation toward Palm Beach County and reported that weather conditions were deteriorating. The crew told air traffic control that there was icing and turbulence, asking the controller if there was a "better ride" ahead.

Fox News' Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

title: Democrats could create 'angry' 'single-issue' voters in 2028 if they remove school choice, CEO warns
excerpt:
The CEO of American Federation for Children, Tommy Schultz, warned Democrats could cause a red wave backlash in 2028 if they remove school choice policies.

The CEO of America’s largest school choice ...
body_text:
The CEO of American Federation for Children, Tommy Schultz, warned Democrats could cause a red wave backlash in 2028 if they remove school choice policies.

The CEO of America’s largest school choice advocacy organization is warning Democrats that abolishing existing universal school choice programs could trigger a major voter backlash in the 2028 elections.

"Put yourself into the shoes of a lower-income mother who is a single parent. She has two or three kids that now just got access into a great private school or a great homeschooling environment that she couldn't afford otherwise without a state program like in Texas, and suddenly, the new wave of people that maybe she even voted for is saying, 'I want to take those options away from your kid immediately and put them back into the school that they've hated,'" American Federation for Children CEO Tommy Schultz told Fox News Digital. "That you've been begging the school district to change policies about … You're now going to tell them you got to go back to that school? They're going to become a single-issue voter in 2028 and vote you out of office."

"I think a lot of these folks that just won office need to be really careful with trying to threaten taking away a family from an educational setting that their kids are thriving in that they're loving, that they're feeling safe in," he added. "That's fundamentally what's at issue here."

DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT

Texas Democratic gubernatorial nominee state Rep. Gina Hinojosa speaks during an education town hall at a local community center on Oct. 10, 2026 in Cypress, Texas. (Danielle Villasana/Getty Images)

Schultz’s comments followed recent midterm election gains by Democrats that have put landmark Republican education policies into question. Republican governors across the country previously passed universal school choice and parental rights measures as post-COVID culture war debates intensified and enrollments declined in major metropolitan public school districts.

In Texas, Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa signaled her intent to reverse school choice expansion upon taking office.

11TH-HOUR POWER PLAY TARGETS INCOMING DEM GOVERNOR AFTER HISTORIC GOP DEFEAT

"It is a victory for the parents of Texas. We are taking our children’s education back from a government that has failed them," Hinojosa said during her victory speech. "Schools will not be taken out of our control, shuttered or suffocated. Being a parent is hard enough without carrying the burdens of a government’s failures. To the children of Texas: Your schools will not close."

The renewed clash over vouchers comes as major urban districts navigate shifting enrollment dynamics. Big-city public school systems across the nation have struggled to retain students as families seek alternative options outside their neighborhood assignments.

NUMBER OF K-12 PUBLIC SCHOOL STUDENTS HAS DECLINED IN MORE THAN HALF OF STATES, REPORT INDICATES

In Texas, for example, the Houston Independent School District board previously voted unanimously to close 12 campuses, citing declining enrollment.

"On day one, I will fire [Texas Education Agency Commissioner] Mike Morath, and we will work tirelessly to repair the damage of the Texas voucher scam, and end an era in which our schools are sold for parts," Hinojosa added during her victory remarks.

Texas GOP Gov. Greg Abbott signed the landmark universal school choice bill in 2025. (Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)

A BLUE WAVE IN GOVERNORS' MANSIONS COULD HURT FAMILIES MORE THAN A BLUE CONGRESS

Voucher and school choice programs face similar legislative challenges following Democratic victories in states like Iowa, Georgia and Nevada.

Schultz predicted that attempts to roll back school choice legislation could ignite a new wave of parental rights activism. Conservative victories in school board races in recent cycles underscored how parents began paying closer attention to local governance, challenging progressive curricula, and voicing strong opposition to explicit content and LGBTQ-related books in classrooms.

MOMS FOR LIBERTY UNLEASHES AI WATCHDOG ON 13,000 SCHOOL DISTRICTS TO FLAG CONTROVERSIAL POLICIES BEFORE VOTES

Conservative political action committees have significantly expanded their footprint in local education contests since 2022. The Virginia-based American Principles Project (APP) first engaged in Florida school board races that year, funding attack ads targeting critical race theory and gender ideology. The APP and the 1776 Project PAC remain among the prominent conservative groups working to shape national education policy.

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, school board meetings have frequently turned into high-profile clashes over parental authority in public education. Schultz foresees similar grassroots pushback if choice options are eliminated.

DENVER MOTHER FIGHTS FOR HER DAUGHTER'S EDUCATION AS ADVOCATES MAKE NATIONWIDE SCHOOL CHOICE PUSH

"If you're going to take away something from parents that they're really loving—like especially something as emotional as the school that your kid is going to—they’re going to get quite angry," Schultz said. "That's where you've seen these movements, in Florida, where these parents rose up against candidates or even court cases where they tried to take hundreds of thousands of kids out of the schools they loved and put 'em back in the schools that they hated. They became single-issue voters."

The broader parental rights movement led several Republican governors to codify parental bills of rights in recent years. Political analysts frequently point to parental rights platforms as key drivers in the election campaigns of figures like former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.

TRUMP EDUCATION OFFICIAL SAYS SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM WILL PUT PRESSURE ON DEM-LED STATE

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis championed parental rights and backed school board candidates that aligned with his agenda. (Paul Hennessy/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

"If you look at the headlines from that 2018 race with Governor Ron DeSantis, the school choice moms tipped the Florida race for him," Schultz said. "That's the type of thing we're talking about that could happen to a lot of these candidates who maybe won on affordability, but they won maybe on small margins, particularly in these state legislative races."

"Don't overread your mandate to suddenly say, 'I want to wipe out a really popular program with parents,'" he added.

Hinojosa did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Joshua Q. Nelson is a reporter for Fox News Digital.

Joshua focuses on cultural trends, education, and public policy. He extensively covered reparations developments across the U.S., the Department of Education, and immigration issues.

Joining Fox News Digital in 2019, he previously graduated from Syracuse University's Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs and received the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton Public Policy Certificate.

Story tips can be sent to joshua.nelson@fox.com and Joshua can be followed on Instagram, Twitter and LinkedIn.

title: Cameroon sets date for twice-delayed legislative and local elections
excerpt:
Cameroon’s President Paul Biya has announced that legislative and local elections will be held in the country on February 7 next year.

Biya, who is 93, made the announcement in a decree read on publi...
body_text:
Cameroon’s President Paul Biya has announced that legislative and local elections will be held in the country on February 7 next year.

Biya, who is 93, made the announcement in a decree read on public radio on Monday.

The decree comes at a tense moment for Cameroon, with authorities cracking down on the opposition, roughly a year after an election that handed Biya another term.

Biya, who has ruled Cameroon since 1982, is the world’s oldest head of state.

His re-election in October last year set off widespread protests that the authorities met with a violent crackdown.

Lawyers cited by Human Rights Watch said security forces detained up to 2,000 people, and some of those detained remain in custody, according to the AFP news agency.

Biya’s government has already postponed Cameroon’s legislative and local elections twice, forcing the extension of lawmakers’ terms to December 20 and those of municipal councillors to February 28, 2027.

The country is also awaiting a government reshuffle announced nearly a year ago and the appointment of a vice president. A constitutional reform reintroduced the post in April, and its holder would be expected to succeed Biya in the event of his death.

Questions about the president’s health have continued to swirl, with his frequent stays abroad fuelling debate over his ability to govern. Media debate about the president’s health, however, has been banned since 2024, when rumours circulated about his death.

In late August, Biya returned to Yaounde after more than two months in Geneva, drawing sharp criticism from the opposition.

Last month, the authorities suspended the Cameroon National Salvation Front (FSNC), the party of defeated opposition presidential candidate Issa Tchiroma Bakary.

Bakary went into exile in the Gambia after declaring himself the election winner and calling on supporters to defend his “victory”.
